stem: Which of the following is FALSE in regards to medication use in pregnancy?

options.html: With few exceptions, poor control of disease tends to have greater impact on pregnancy outcome than drug therapies
Clearance of most drugs is increased in pregnancy
Conversations surrounding the teratogenicity of drugs should occur at ~8 weeks gestation, before organogenesis begins
Effective drugs that have been used for longer periods of time are preferable to newer drugs
Use of drugs in pregnancy should be minimized to only those that are necessary and for the shortest period of time possible

answer: The correct answer is C. Two things are wrong with it. Conversations about teratogenicity should occur at the time of prescription in any woman of childbearing age — not once she is already pregnant. And the majority of organogenesis has already occurred by 8 weeks, so 8 weeks is not "before organogenesis begins".

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q85-Q87. Tests [[03 - Teratogenesis]], [[10 - Drugs Used in Gynecology]].
stem: Maria is a 24 y.o. woman with a history of depression who comes to you with a positive pregnancy test. Her depression has been well controlled on Fluoxetine, an SSRI antidepressant, for the past 6 years. She worries about the effect of this medication - what should you do?

options.html: Antidepressants are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy, stop the drug immediately and refer to a psychologist for counseling in order to control her depression during her pregnancy
Fluoxetine is associated with malformations, therefore you should start her on a newer antidepressant which has not yet been shown to be associated with birth defects
In order to avoid withdrawal of both Maria and the fetus from the antidepressant, you should wean her off the drug slowly and remain drug-free for the duration of the pregnancy
Start another agent such as valproic acid in order achieve optimum control of her depression and prevent any deterioration during her pregnancy
Stay on the same dose of fluoxetine to maintain control of her depression

answer:
The correct answer is E. Depression in pregnancy is itself associated with bad outcomes, so maintaining treatment matters. Fluoxetine has been studied, and malformations arise at the same rate in fluoxetine-exposed women as in the general population.

B inverts the correct principle (see Q85D): it is better to use effective drugs with a long track record than newer alternatives that have not been studied as extensively. D is actively dangerous — valproic acid is known to cause neural tube defects and should not be added to a pregnant woman's regimen unless completely necessary.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q85-Q87. Tests [[03 - Teratogenesis]], [[10 - Drugs Used in Gynecology]].
stem: Which of the following drugs is NOT a known teratogen?
answer: The correct answer is D. Acetaminophen is the safe one; warfarin, lithium, misoprostol and ethanol are all known teratogens.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter only.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q90, Q104-Q106. Tests [[02 - Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada]].
stem: Which of the following soft markers of aneuploidy is most strongly associated with fetal morbidity?
answer:
The correct answer is A. A thickened nuchal fold is associated with Down syndrome and carries an odds ratio of 20-25x.

Do not confuse the two nuchal measurements: nuchal fold thickness is measured on the second-trimester scan (~18-22 weeks); nuchal translucency is measured in the first trimester (see Q104).

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q90, Q104-Q106. Tests [[02 - Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada]].
stem: An increased nuchal translucency may suggest:
answer:
The correct answer is A. Nuchal translucency is a component of integrated prenatal screening and an effective screening tool for chromosomal abnormalities and congenital malformations. Increased NT can also be present in a normal pregnancy.

D is the exception to note: although IPS overall has a high detection rate for neural tube defects, NT measurement alone is not effective in detecting NTDs. See prenatal screening.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q90, Q104-Q106. Tests [[02 - Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada]].
stem: Which of the following tests is useful for prenatal diagnosis:
answer:
The correct answer is E. The question hinges on diagnosis vs. screening:

  • DIAGNOSTIC: amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling, ultrasound
  • SCREENING: IPS, nuchal translucency, soft markers, serum screening

Only E is a diagnostic test. See prenatal screening.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q90, Q104-Q106. Tests [[02 - Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada]].
stem: Which of the following patients should be offered prenatal diagnosis by invasive testing?

options.html: 24-year-old G1P0 with a previous history of one early pregnancy loss
29-year-old G3P2 with a family history of T2DM
19-year-old primigravida woman with a normal prenatal screen
31-year-old G2P1 whose partner is a balanced translocation carrier

answer:
The correct answer is E. Indications for prenatal diagnosis by invasive testing:

  • Advanced maternal age (>37 years) — note that makes A, at 35, insufficient
  • Previous child with a chromosome abnormality
  • A parent is a balanced translocation carrier
  • Family history of a genetic disorder diagnosable prenatally
  • Positive findings on prenatal screen or ultrasound

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q91-Q94. Tests [[07 - Approach to First Trimester Bleeding & Ultrasound]], [[08 - Pathology of 1st Trimester Bleeding]].
stem: What is the most commonly known cause of spontaneous abortion?
answer: The correct answer is D. Approximately 15-20% of all clinical pregnancies end in spontaneous abortion. In most cases the cause is unknown — but when the cause is known, the most common contributor is an inherent abnormality of the fetus. Note the careful wording of the question: "most commonly known cause".

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q91-Q94. Tests [[07 - Approach to First Trimester Bleeding & Ultrasound]], [[08 - Pathology of 1st Trimester Bleeding]].
stem: What is the normal doubling time of hCG in a healthy early pregnancy?
answer: The correct answer is D. Normal doubling time in early pregnancy (<10 weeks) is about 48-72 hours. If hCG rises less than 85% over 48 hours, there is a greater association with abnormal pregnancy.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q91-Q94. Tests [[07 - Approach to First Trimester Bleeding & Ultrasound]], [[08 - Pathology of 1st Trimester Bleeding]].
stem: What is the most common cause of ectopic pregnancy?

options.html: Use of an intra-uterine contraceptive device (IUD)

answer:
The correct answer is B. PID — including puerperal and post-abortal sepsis — is the #1 cause of ectopic pregnancy.

A is the classic trap: a pregnancy in an IUD user is more likely to be ectopic, because the device protects against an intrauterine pregnancy specifically. But pregnancy in an IUD user is rare, so the IUD is not a common cause of ectopics.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q91-Q94. Tests [[07 - Approach to First Trimester Bleeding & Ultrasound]], [[08 - Pathology of 1st Trimester Bleeding]].
stem: What diagnosis is suggested by the following pathological findings: large hydropic villi involving all tissue, trophoblast proliferation?
answer:
The correct answer is B. A complete molar pregnancy occurs when both chromosome sets are of paternal origin. Diagnosis is made clinically but confirmed histologically.

Complete molePartial mole
Fetusabsentabnormal fetus may be present
Villilarge, swollen, hydropic — ALL tissuesmaller hydropic villi interspersed with normal villi
Trophoblast proliferationmarkedless

See gestational trophoblastic disease.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q89, Q95, Q98. Tests [[04 - Topics of Antenatal Care]], [[09 - Second Trimester Ultrasound]].
stem: Routine morphology is performed via ultrasound at 18-20 weeks gestation. What is the prevalence of major anomalies found in the general population?
answer: The correct answer is B. 2-3%.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter only.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q89, Q95, Q98. Tests [[04 - Topics of Antenatal Care]], [[09 - Second Trimester Ultrasound]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT a common symptom/complaint in a pregnant woman at 34 weeks gestation?
answer: The correct answer is C. Nausea and vomiting are much more common in the first trimester and are usually not present in the third. All the other listed complaints are common in the third trimester.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q89, Q95, Q98. Tests [[04 - Topics of Antenatal Care]], [[09 - Second Trimester Ultrasound]].
stem: Which of the following fetal assessment tools is the most predictive of perinatal mortality?
answer:
The correct answer is B. FMC, NST and BPP all provide helpful information but really only give a "snapshot" of what is happening with the fetus, and have no effect on perinatal mortality rate.

Umbilical artery Doppler, by contrast, is predictive of morbidity and mortality — and if normal, is associated with a decreased PMR.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q77, Q100-Q103. Tests [[11 - Hypertension in Pregnancy]].
stem: A 28-year-old primigravida presents to the obstetrics clinic at 24 weeks gestation with complaints of headache and blurred vision. On examination, her blood pressure is 150/100 mmHg and her urine dipstick reveals 2+ proteinuria. Which of the following is a likely consequence of the abnormality of uterine spiral arteries seen in this patient?

options.html: Increased risk of fetal growth restriction
Increased risk of preterm premature rupture of membranes

answer:
The correct answer is C. This is pre-eclampsia — hypertension plus proteinuria developing after 20 weeks. One of the underlying mechanisms is thought to be abnormal remodeling of the uterine spiral arteries, which leads to inadequate blood flow to the placenta and therefore impaired fetal growth.

Fetal growth restriction is a common complication of pre-eclampsia and can cause significant morbidity and mortality if not managed, which is why close monitoring matters. Note that A and B are both the wrong direction — pre-eclampsia increases the risk of preterm labour and abruption.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q77, Q100-Q103. Tests [[11 - Hypertension in Pregnancy]].
stem: Which of the following describes normal variations in blood pressure throughout pregnancy?

options.html: BP falls to lowest point in T1, increases slightly in T2 and rises to highest level in T3
BP remains normal during T1, falls in T2, and returns to normal at term
BP remains normal during T1, falls in T2, and increases to hypertension in T3
BP increases in T1, remains high in T2, and falls to lowest levels near term
Blood pressure should remain steady during pregnancy

answer: The correct answer is B. Blood pressure normally drops in the second trimester, because pregnant women are relatively vasodilated — but BP should return to normal at term. Option C is the trap: a rise to hypertension in T3 is pathological (pre-eclampsia), not a normal variation.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q77, Q100-Q103. Tests [[11 - Hypertension in Pregnancy]].
stem: A 24-year-old primigravid woman presents at 34 weeks after a normal course of pregnancy. She is now presenting with weight gain of 6 lb. in the past 2 weeks. Her BP is 148/100, and her urine contains 2+ protein. The best management of this woman is:

options.html: Ensure fetal well-being, rule out adverse conditions and deliver at term
Induction of labour regardless of gestational age
Monitor fetal well-being and, and administer MgSO4 and antihypertensives

answer:
The correct answer is C. This woman has mild pre-eclampsia (BP >140/90, proteinuria >1+). Management: identify the underlying cause, rule out adverse conditions, ensure fetal wellbeing, increase maternal/fetal surveillance, and deliver at term if investigations are normal.

D and E are the severe pre-eclampsia answers: delivery regardless of gestational age, plus antihypertensives and MgSO4. Compare directly with Q102, where the numbers are severe.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q77, Q100-Q103. Tests [[11 - Hypertension in Pregnancy]].
stem: A 30-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks gestation presents with a blood pressure of 160/110 mmHg and 4+ proteinuria. Which of the following is NOT a recommended initial management option for this patient?

options.html: Administration of magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis
Initiation of antihypertensive therapy to lower blood pressure
Delivery of the fetus and placenta as soon as possible
Hospitalization for close monitoring and management

answer:
The correct answer is C. This patient has severe pre-eclampsia — defined as BP ≥ 160/110 mmHg with 4+ proteinuria. Initial management is MgSO4 for seizure prophylaxis, antihypertensives if needed, and hospitalization for close monitoring.

Delivery is the definitive treatment, but not an initial management option — the timing must be weighed against gestational age and disease severity. In general, delivery is recommended after 34 weeks; earlier only if needed to prevent maternal or fetal complications. At 33 weeks, "as soon as possible" is premature.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q77, Q100-Q103. Tests [[11 - Hypertension in Pregnancy]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT considered a risk factor for the development of preeclampsia?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Risk factors for pre-eclampsia: age <20 or >35, BMI >35, hypertension, renal disease, diabetes, connective tissue disease, previous pre-eclampsia, first pregnancies or pregnancies after an interval of >10 years, and multiple gestations.

Age 33 falls inside the safe window (neither <20 nor >35) — that's the whole point of the option. Note BMI 36 clears the >35 threshold.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q80, Q121. Tests [[01 - Antepartum Hemorrhage & Abnormal Placentation]].
stem: Which of the following placental abnormalities may occur from the placenta being implanted too shallowly in the uterus?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Sort the options by what went wrong with implantation:

  • Too deeply → accreta, increta, percreta
  • Wrong location (obstructing the cervical os) → previa
  • Too shallowly → abruption, because a shallowly implanted placenta is more likely to detach from the uterine wall — which can cause hemorrhage, shock, and both fetal and maternal death.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q80, Q121. Tests [[01 - Antepartum Hemorrhage & Abnormal Placentation]].
stem: Fetal cells present in the maternal circulation on a Kleihauer Betke test suggests
answer: The correct answer is C. Placental abruption.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter only. The logic: the Kleihauer-Betke test detects fetal red cells that have crossed into maternal blood, which requires a breach of the fetomaternal interface — i.e. the placenta shearing away from the uterine wall.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q96-Q97. Tests [[02 - Approach to the Small Fetus]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT a common fetal risk in post-term pregnancy?
answer:
The correct answer is A. Post-term pregnancy is defined as pregnancy extending beyond 42 weeks. Risks include macrosomia, birth trauma (shoulder dystocia, prolonged labour, operative delivery), post-maturity syndrome and death.

The direction is the discriminator: post-term pregnancy causes oligohydramnios, not polyhydramnios — which can in turn cause complications such as intolerance of labour.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q96-Q97. Tests [[02 - Approach to the Small Fetus]].
stem: An ultrasound is performed to assess fetal growth and reports an asymmetric intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). The most likely diagnosis is:
answer:
The correct answer is A. Split IUGR by symmetry:

  • Asymmetric — 70-80% of cases; caused by uteroplacental insufficiency (abruption, circumvallate placenta, etc.)
  • Symmetric — 20-30% of cases; most often caused by an early severe insult such as infection or chromosomal abnormality

The logic: a late insult spares the already-grown head (asymmetric); an early insult stunts everything at once (symmetric).

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q108-Q110. Tests [[03 - Approach to Preterm Labor]].
stem: Which of the following is the strongest risk factor for premature labour?
answer:
The correct answer is B. A previous premature delivery is the strongest risk factor for premature labour:

  • 15% risk with 1 previous preterm birth
  • 30% risk with 2 previous preterm births

Other important risk factors: PROM, indications for preterm induction including pre-eclampsia, multiple gestation and placental abnormalities. But 50% of all preterm deliveries have no identifiable cause.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q108-Q110. Tests [[03 - Approach to Preterm Labor]].
stem: A 32 year-old primigravida woman presents to the emergency department with premature rupture of membranes at 37 weeks gestation. She does not have a fever and has not yet experienced any contractions. Appropriate management at this time is:

options.html: Tocolysis for 48-72 hours to allow for transfer to birth unit
Observation for spontaneous onset of labour
Immediate induction of labour and administration of MgSO4 and antenatal steroids
Urgent Caesarean section followed by administration of antibiotics
Insertion of an intrauterine pressure monitor

answer:
The correct answer is B. At 37 weeks this is TERM PROM without labour — the gestational age is the whole question. Management of term PROM: allow spontaneous labour, induce with oxytocin at ~6 h if labour does not begin naturally, and GBS prophylaxis.

Contrast the two things the distractors describe:

  • Preterm PROM → antibiotic therapy, antenatal steroids, induction at ~36 weeks
  • Preterm labour → tocolysis × 48 h, antenatal betamethasone, GBS prophylaxis

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q108-Q110. Tests [[03 - Approach to Preterm Labor]].
stem: Which of the following is not a risk factor for preterm labour?
answer:
The correct answer is D. First pregnancy is not a risk factor for preterm labour.

Note that this cuts against the intuition built in Q103, where first pregnancy is a risk factor — for pre-eclampsia. Different outcome, different risk profile.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q111-Q115. Tests [[04 - Process of Labor and Birth]].
stem: The cardinal movements of normal labour in CORRECT ORDER are:

options.html: Engagement, Flexion, Descent, Extension, Internal Rotation, External Rotation, Expulsion
Engagement, Descent, Flexion, Internal Rotation, Extension, External Rotation, Expulsion.
Descent, Engagement, Flexion, Extension, Internal Rotation, External Rotation, Expulsion.
Descent, Engagement, Internal Rotation, Flexion, External Rotation, Extension, Expulsion.
Engagement, Descent, Flexion, Internal Rotation, External Rotation, Flexion, Extension, Expulsion.

answer: The correct answer is B. Engagement → Descent → Flexion → Internal Rotation → Extension → External Rotation → Expulsion.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter only. The discriminators across the options: engagement precedes descent (eliminates C and D), flexion precedes internal rotation (eliminates A and D), and extension precedes external rotation (eliminates E, which also lists flexion twice).

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q111-Q115. Tests [[04 - Process of Labor and Birth]].
stem: Which of the following does NOT contribute to the initiation of labour?

options.html: High levels of progesterone at term

answer:
The correct answer is D. Progesterone is high throughout pregnancy, but is decreased relative to estrogen at term. It is therefore progesterone withdrawal that initiates labour — not high progesterone levels.

The genuine contributors: oxytocin, prostaglandin, withdrawal of relaxin and prostacyclin, and fetal triggers such as HPA axis activation.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q111-Q115. Tests [[04 - Process of Labor and Birth]].
stem: The second stage of labour is defined as:

options.html: Onset of labour to full dilatation
Cervical dilation of 5 cm with regular uterine contractions
Full dilation to delivery of fetus
Autotransfusion and hemodynamic shift occurring after birth

answer: The correct answer is C. Second stage = full dilation → delivery of the fetus.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter only. For the full set: first stage = onset of labour → full dilatation (option A); third stage = delivery of the fetus → expulsion of the placenta (see Q115).

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q111-Q115. Tests [[04 - Process of Labor and Birth]].
stem: The target nerves for pain control during the first stage of labour are:
answer: The correct answer is B. First-stage pain is best controlled by targeting T10-T12. This pain is often experienced as back pain, which is the clue to its level. Options for pain control in labour: epidural, pudendal block, general anesthetic, Lamaze breathing.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q111-Q115. Tests [[04 - Process of Labor and Birth]].
stem: The active management of the third stage of labour includes:

options.html: Oxytocin infusion, cord traction, fundal massage
Maternal surveillance for complications related to autotransfusion
Assessment of cervical length and administration of progesterone
Insertion of an intrauterine pressure catheter

answer:
The correct answer is A. The third stage runs from delivery of the fetus to expulsion of the placenta. Per WHO guidelines, active management of placental delivery includes:

  • Uterotonic agents (oxytocin/ergot)
  • Gentle traction of the umbilical cord
  • Fundal massage, to prevent inversion of the uterus

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q88, Q99, Q123, Q137. Tests [[05 - Abnormal Labor]].
stem: Contraindications to labour and vaginal delivery include:
answer: The correct answer is E. All four are contraindications to labour and vaginal delivery: placenta previa, abnormal fetal lie, active genital herpes, and a prior classical caesarean (a vertical uterine incision, which carries a far higher rupture risk than the usual low transverse incision).

flags.title: Workbook error — the explanation belongs to a different question
flags.html:
The key reads in full: "88. Answer: E and 40% fetal). 16.7 lb. should go to the maternal component of the weight gain->to uterus, breasts, blood, water, fat. The other 10.6lb goes to fetal component->fetus, placenta, amniotic fluid."

That is a stray fragment about the distribution of pregnancy weight gain (~60% maternal / 40% fetal), which has nothing to do with contraindications to vaginal delivery. The letter E is correct; the explanation above is reconstructed. The orphaned fact is still worth knowing: of ~27 lb total gain, 16.7 lb is maternal (uterus, breasts, blood, water, fat) and 10.6 lb is fetal (fetus, placenta, amniotic fluid).

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q88, Q99, Q123, Q137. Tests [[05 - Abnormal Labor]].
stem: Management of macrosomia in pregnancy should include all of the following EXCEPT:

options.html: Induction of labour at term with favourable cervix

answer:
The correct answer is C. Umbilical artery Doppler is an important tool for assessing growth restriction — but it is not needed in macrosomia, because placental insufficiency is not the concern here. This is the mirror image of Q98.

Management of macrosomia: rule out causes including gestational diabetes, review nutrition and exercise to manage weight gain, U/S assessment of weight, and possible induction at term if the cervix is favourable. It may also include caesarean section for fetal weight >5 kg, or >4.5 kg in diabetic mothers.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q88, Q99, Q123, Q137. Tests [[05 - Abnormal Labor]].
stem: A 28-year-old nulliparous woman at term presents in active labor with cervical dilation of 8 cm. The fetal heart rate tracing shows a Category II pattern. Which of the following is an appropriate next step in management?

options.html: Continue labor and re-evaluate the fetal heart rate tracing in 30 minutes
Administer a bolus of crystalloid fluid and position the patient in the left lateral decubitus position
Attempt operative vaginal delivery with forceps or vacuum extraction

answer:
The correct answer is A. Fetal heart rate tracings are categorized I, II or III. A Category II pattern is indeterminate and requires further evaluation and consideration of interventions — not immediate action.

The appropriate next step is to continue labour and re-evaluate the tracing in 30 minutes, which allows time for the fetus to recover from transient hypoxic episodes and for labour to progress. If the tracing remains Category II or worsens to Category III, further interventions — amnioinfusion, fetal scalp sampling, or expedited delivery — may become necessary.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q88, Q99, Q123, Q137. Tests [[05 - Abnormal Labor]].
stem: Which of the following scenarios are NOT an indication for a C-section?
answer:
The correct answer is A. The full list of indications for a C/S: abnormal FHR, fetal malpresentation (e.g. breech), dystocia, maternal HSV/HIV infection, fetal congenital abnormalities, abnormal placentation (e.g. abruption), masses, multiple gestation, cervical cancer.

Maternal diabetes is not itself an indication — though note from Q99 that a diabetic mother with an estimated fetal weight >4.5 kg may need one for macrosomia.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q107. Tests [[06 - Hemorrhagic Schock]].
stem: Which of the following is/are true regarding post-partum hemorrhage?

options.html: >500 ml blood loss for C-section or >1000 ml for vaginal delivery
Most common cause of maternal mortality worldwide
Sheehan's syndrome is a potential complication
Oxytocin is used for prevention of PPH only

answer:
The correct answer is G (B and C). Both distractor statements are true-sounding but have a detail flipped:

  • A has the thresholds swapped. PPH is >1000 mL for C-section or >500 mL for vaginal delivery — or loss of any volume that causes hemodynamic instability.
  • D is wrong because of the word "only". Oxytocin is used for prevention of PPH and as a uterotonic agent to treat an atonic uterus during active hemorrhage.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q116, Q120, Q125. Tests [[08 - Postpartum Care]].
stem: Which of the following statements is true of "post-partum blues"?

options.html: Mood changes associated with post-partum blues are generally self-limited.
The most common time to experience post-partum blues is approximately 2-4 weeks following delivery.
Symptoms of post-partum blues often include extreme disinterest in the baby and suicidal or homicidal ideation.

answer:
The correct answer is A. Every wrong option is a postpartum depression fact mislabelled as blues — that is the entire question:

Post-partum bluesPost-partum depression
Frequency~85% of women (so C's 15% is wrong)10-20%
Onsetday 3-10 (so B's 2-4 weeks is wrong)within 6 months of delivery
Courseself-limited, lasts ~2 weeksas for depression
Severe features—disinterest in the baby, homicidal or suicidal ideation (so D is wrong)
Treatment—antidepressants + counselling/therapy

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q116, Q120, Q125. Tests [[08 - Postpartum Care]].
stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to your office 6 weeks post partum, after giving birth to a healthy baby boy. She has been doing generally well but has noticed that recently she is experiencing pain in her nipples during breastfeeding, and that her nipples appear to be cracked and dry. She has continued with breastfeeding despite this change. Her infant son has been doing well, although she does state that he appears to have patchy white spots on the inside of his mouth. What is the most appropriate management of this patient's problem?

options.html: Topical nystatin to the nipple and infant's mouth
Continue breastfeeding, heat application to breast, fluids, rest

answer:
The correct answer is B. The white patches in the infant's mouth, plus cracked nipples and pain with feeding, make this a candidal infection. Management is topical nystatin cream to the infant's mouth and the areola after each feed for 2 weeks, then qhs for another 2 weeks.

E is the near-miss: oral fluconazole is another option but is not the most appropriate, because it is associated with serious side effects. A treats breast engorgement. C (plus antibiotics) is the treatment for mastitis.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q116, Q120, Q125. Tests [[08 - Postpartum Care]].
stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department 4 days after a vaginal delivery with complaints of heavy vaginal bleeding. She has been passing clots and soaking through 2 pads per hour for the past 12 hours. She denies fever, chills, or abdominal pain. On physical exam, the uterus is tender and enlarged to the level of the umbilicus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is D — but the workbook contradicts itself here.

The misplaced explanation is still worth keeping for its own content: PPH is >500 mL after vaginal delivery or >1000 mL after caesarean (compare Q107). The most common cause of PPH is uterine atony — a soft, boggy, poorly contracted uterus that fails to achieve hemostasis at the placental attachment site. Risk factors for atony: prolonged labour, multiple gestation, macrosomia, chorioamnionitis. Retained placenta or membranes can also cause PPH but is less likely given the 4-day timing and absence of fever.

flags.title: Workbook error — the key's explanations are off by one from Q125 onward
flags.html:
The key states only "125. Answer: D" (endometritis) with no explanation. It then attaches to Q126 an explanation that reads "126. Answer: B. Uterine atony. Postpartum hemorrhage is defined as blood loss of greater than 500 mL after vaginal delivery... In the scenario described, the patient presents with heavy vaginal bleeding, clots, and uterine tenderness and enlargement, which are all consistent with uterine atony."

That explanation is unmistakably about this question, not Q126 (which asks about fetal energy sources) — and it argues for B, uterine atony, directly contradicting the letter D printed against Q125. The drift continues: Q144's explanation is the answer to Q126. So from here the key's letters stay aligned but its prose runs one question behind.

Which is right? The clinical details favour the printed D: PPH at 4 days is secondary PPH, and uterine tenderness is the endometritis finding. True uterine atony causes primary PPH within 24 h and gives a soft, boggy uterus — the misplaced explanation even says "soft, boggy... poorly contracted", which does not match this stem's tender, enlarged uterus. The explanation also concedes that endometritis "may cause uterine tenderness" but dismisses it for absence of fever. Treat D as the answer and B as a defensible distractor; verify against a real source.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q117-Q119. Tests [[09 - Lactation]].
stem: The three factors necessary for lactation are:
answer: The correct answer is D. Prolactin (anterior pituitary) and oxytocin (posterior pituitary) are the endocrine triggers necessary for milk production. Milk removal — by infant or pump — is the third factor, and must begin by day 3 after birth to drive lactogenesis forward. See 09 - Lactation.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q117-Q119. Tests [[09 - Lactation]].
stem: Which of the following is a contraindication to breastfeeding?

options.html: HIV infection in a developing country

answer:
The correct answer is D. Active psychosis is a contraindication to breastfeeding, because of the risk of the mother harming the baby.

A is deliberately qualified: HIV infection is a contraindication in developed countries, but not in underdeveloped countries, because there the risks of GI disease/infection from formula outweigh the risk of HIV transmission. Smoking, alcohol and SSRI use are not contraindications, although smoking is strongly discouraged.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q117-Q119. Tests [[09 - Lactation]].
stem: What is the significance of the first 4-6 minutes of each breastfeeding?

options.html: The first 4-6 minutes of each feed contains the highest content of fat, therefore promoting infant satiety and maternal weight loss after pregnancy.
The first 4-6 minutes of each feed has the most impact on hormonal levels, leading to more effective contraception in the post-partum period.
Failure to breastfeed longer than 4-6 minutes at each feed may contribute to breast engorgement and blocked ducts.
The first 4-6 minutes of each feed contains the highest amount of protein.

answer: The correct answer is D. The breast milk in the first 4-6 minutes of each feed contains the majority of the protein for that feed. After this point the milk becomes richer in fat, which promotes satiety — so A has the order exactly backwards.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q122, Q124, Q127. Tests [[07 - Approach to Neonatal Care]].
stem: The primary reason that APGAR scores are recorded in newborns is

options.html: To assess the need for resuscitation
To assess the probability of perinatal morbidity
To provide a common measurement to be used in research studies

answer: The correct answer is A. APGAR scores are used primarily to assess the need for resuscitation, and to monitor the effect of resuscitative efforts over time. They are not predictive of future IQ.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q122, Q124, Q127. Tests [[07 - Approach to Neonatal Care]].
stem: If present after 7 months, which of the following reflexes suggests cerebral palsy?
answer: The correct answer is B. The ATNR or "fencing" reflex is present in newborns and should be gone by 6 months of age. Its presence after 7 months is ALWAYS abnormal, and typically suggests cerebral palsy.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q122, Q124, Q127. Tests [[07 - Approach to Neonatal Care]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT part of the appropriate management of a case of neonatal sepsis?
answer: The correct answer is C. Expectant management is NEVER part of the management of neonatal sepsis. The infant should be started on broad-spectrum antibiotics, which may be narrowed once blood culture results are available.

stem: You are brushing up on your anatomy in your spare time by browsing an online anatomy library. You come across a specimen depicting the superficial perineal space. However, you know that this specimen was labeled incorrectly because you are able to see:
answer:
The correct answer is E. The urogenital diaphragm is in the deep perineal space, and contains the perineal membrane, voluntary muscle and deep perineal fascia.

The superficial perineal space contains: ischiocavernosus muscle, bulbospongiosus muscle, superficial transverse perineal muscle, crura of the penis or vagina, bulb of the penis (males), vestibular bulbs and greater vestibular glands (females). See 06 - Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function.

stem: Which of the following is responsible for the remodeling of the uterine spiral arteries?
answer: The correct answer is A. Extravillous trophoblasts invade the uterine wall, enter the existing arteries, and induce apoptosis in the smooth muscle cells lining the endothelium of the spiral arteries. That apoptosis forms a new lining to the artery, which is the remodeling.

stem: What is the purpose of uterine artery remodeling during pregnancy?

options.html: To allow for detachment of the placenta after labour
To maintain an adequately high blood pressure
To lower blood pressure and allow adequate blood flow to the fetus
To increase blood flow in the mother by decreasing the oxygen demand of the placenta and fetus
To allow for regular fluctuations in blood supply to the placenta and fetus

answer: The correct answer is C. Remodeling of the spiral arteries produces large-bore, low-resistance vessels, which supply more blood to the fetus. This is the physiology whose failure produces pre-eclampsia — compare Q77.

stem: Which of the following should be used in the prevention of pre-eclampsia in low risk women?
answer:
The correct answer is E. Calcium supplementation is useful in both high- and low-risk women if dietary calcium intake is low.

There is no role for salt restriction, dietary modification or antioxidants in preventing pre-eclampsia. D is the near-miss: low-dose ASA is useful in women with risk factors, but is not used routinely in low-risk women — and "low risk" is the operative phrase in the stem.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (13 questions). Delivered in Asynch W4.
stem: Which of the following are physiological actions of both estrogen and progesterone? Select all that apply.

options.html: They stimulate proliferation of breast cells
They stimulate proliferation of endometrial cells
They alter the release of gonadotrophins (FSH, LH)

answer: The correct answers are A and C. Estrogen and progesterone have opposing actions in many tissues. For example, estrogen stimulates the proliferation of endometrial cells while progesterone stimulates differentiation of these cells. But both hormones have proliferative actions in breast tissue. Both hormones also alter the release of FSH and LH. Estrogen decreases the amount of FSH and LH released (except mid-cycle) while progesterone decreases the frequency of the LH and FSH pulses (except during the luteal phase). Finally, progesterone suppresses uterine contractility.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (13 questions). Delivered in Asynch W4.
stem: Which of the following best describes the primary mechanism of contraceptive actions of the progestin-only preparations?

options.html: Development of an inflammatory process in the uterine cavity

answer: The correct answer is C. Progestin-only contraceptives can decrease the chances of ovulation by altering the frequency of GnRH pulses. However, the suppression of ovulation is more consistent with the combined contraceptive preparations. The contraceptive actions of the POCs rely mostly in the changes that progestins promote in the uterus; it alters tubal peristalsis, it thickens the cervical mucus and creates an endometrium that is not receptive. The development of an inflammatory process in the uterine cavity and spermicide effects are the main contraceptive actions of the copper IUD devices.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (13 questions). Delivered in Asynch W4.
stem: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to the use of combined contraceptives but not progestin-only contraceptive?
answer: The correct answer is D. Breast cancer, undiagnosed bleeding and severe liver failure are contraindications to both combined and progestin-only methods. Hypertension is a relative contraindication that needs to be assessed on a case by case basis. Thomboembolic events are a contraindication for the use of combined contraceptives as the estrogen component seems to increase the risk of developing these events. Progestin-only contraceptives seem to carry no apparent risk of VTE or stroke. Except for drospirenone and cyproterone, the antiandrigenic progestins. There are epidemiological studies suggesting increased risk of VTE and stroke with preparations containing these progestins.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (13 questions). Delivered in Asynch W4.
stem: Which of the following is a unique property of SERMs?

options.html: Act as agonists in some tissues and antagonists in other tissues
Activate a unique plasma membrane-bound receptor
Have both estrogenic and pro gestational agonist activity
Inhibit the aromatase enzyme required for estrogen synthesis
Produce estrogenic effects without binding to estrogen receptors

answer: The correct answer is A. SERMs and SPRMs present tissue-specific actions by modulating the activity of the estrogen and progesterone receptors.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (13 questions). Delivered in Asynch W4.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?

options.html: Ulipristal and Levonorgestrel present similar efficacy when used up to 120 hrs of unprotected intercourse
Ulipristal delays ovation by preventing the LH surge while Levonorgestrel delays ovulation by direct actions in the follicles
Ulipristal and Levonorgestrel present similar efficacy when used up to 72 hrs of unprotected intercourse
Ulipristal and Levonorgestrel are SPRMs with agonistic actions in endometrium
Ulipristal and Levonorgestrel are more effective emergency contraceptive methods than the copper-IUD device

answer: The correct answer is C. When used after 72 hrs of unprotected intercourse, Ulipristal seems to be more efficacious in delaying ovulation than Levonorgestrel. Up to 72 hrs, they have similar efficacy; Ulipristal may be more efficacious. Both of these drugs delay ovulation by suppressing the LH surge. Ulipristal have some direct action in the ovaries that may contribute to prevent follicle rupture. Ulipristal is a SPRM while Levonorgestrel is primarily a progesterone receptor agonist. Copper-IUD devices are more efficacious than the other emergency contraceptive methods. It promotes an inflammatory response in the uterine cavity creating an environment that is not receptive for fertilization and implantation. Copper is also toxic for sperms and blastocyst.

flags.title: ⚠ The module’s key contradicts the lecture’s own slide
flags.html:
The key says UPA and LNG have similar efficacy up to 72 hrs, and the module’s own explanation immediately hedges it (“Up to 72 hrs, they have similar efficacy; Ulipristal may be more efficacious”).

The meta-analysis on slide 43 of the same lecture’s deck has UPA significantly better at every interval, including inside 72 hours: 0–24 h 0.9% vs 2.5% (OR 0.35, p = 0.035), 0–72 h 1.4% vs 2.2% (OR 0.58, p = 0.046), 0–120 h 1.3% vs 2.2% (OR 0.55, p = 0.025). (Glasier et al., Lancet 2010;375(9714):555–62.)

Both are recorded as they stand. The deck’s data is the one to trust, and this is a good one to raise with the facilitator.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (13 questions). Delivered in Asynch W4.
stem: Which of the following best describes the pharmacological basis that supports the use of NSAIDs to treat the symptoms of dysmenorrhea?

options.html: NSAIDs promote a decrease in blood flow
NSAIDs promote a decrease in prostaglandin synthesis
NSAIDs promote a decrease in progesterone synthesis
NSAIDs promote a decrease in trombone A2 synthesis

answer: The correct answer is B. Prostaglandins, released by the endometrial cells, are associated with the symptoms of dysmenorrhea. Prostaglandins promote uterine contraction. NSAIDs reduce the production of prostaglandins by inhibiting the cyclooxigenases enzymes. By doing this, it alleviates the pain associated with the menstrual cramps.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (13 questions). Delivered in Asynch W4.
stem: Which of the following best describes a primary difference between GnRH agonists and GnRH antagonists in terms of their mechanism of action?

options.html: GnRH agonists cause immediate suppression of gonadotropin release, while GnRH antagonists cause an initial flare of gonadotropin release.
Both GnRH agonists and antagonists cause an initial increase in gonadotropin release before suppressing it.
GnRH agonists initially cause an increase in gonadotropin release before desensitizing receptors, while GnRH antagonists immediately block gonadotropin release.
Both GnRH agonists and antagonists have the same effect, but agonists are longer-acting.

answer: The correct answer is C. GnRH agonists initially stimulate the release of gonadotropins (LH and FSH), causing a transient “flare” effect, but eventually desensitize the GnRH receptors, leading to suppression of gonadotropin release. In contrast, GnRH antagonists block GnRH receptors immediately, preventing gonadotropin release without causing a flare.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (13 questions). Delivered in Asynch W4.
stem: Which of the following side effects would you expect with long-term GnRH agonist use?
answer: The correct answer is A. Long-term GnRH agonist use suppresses gonadotropin release, leading to reduced sex hormone production (estrogen and testosterone), which can cause osteoporosis due to decreased bone density (loss of the protective effects of estrogens in bone tissue). The decrease in sex hormones can cause a decrease in libido and muscle mass. The hot flashes are also an expected side effect of long-term use of GnRH agonists as these drugs induce an hypoestrogenic state.

lecture: Concept Checks - Drugs Used in Gynecology
lectureMeta: Source: the lecture's slide deck (Drugs used in gynecology slides.pdf, 57 slides), 2 questions. Neither is keyed on its own slide; both are answered by the slides around them. The deck carries no patient cases.
stem: Which of the following is a relative contraindication to hormonal contraceptives?
answer:
The correct answer is B. The contraindications slide that follows this one lists five items and marks exactly one of them “(relative)” — hypertension. The other four are absolute: breast cancer or another cancer of the reproductive tract, a history of stroke / thromboembolic disease / myocardial infarction / coronary artery disease, severe cirrhosis or liver tumour, and abnormal undiagnosed bleeding. The same slide adds a sixth entry that is neither — CAUTION: smoker >35 years of age.

Hypertension is relative because it is graded and modifiable: it is assessed case by case. Compare with Q7, which asks the mirror-image question — which contraindication applies to combined but not progestin-only methods — and keys it to the active thromboembolic event.

Options copied verbatim from the slide, including the fact that the key is the shortest one. The deck wrote it that way and it is not repaired here.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lecture: Concept Checks - Drugs Used in Gynecology
lectureMeta: Source: the lecture's slide deck (Drugs used in gynecology slides.pdf, 57 slides), 2 questions. Neither is keyed on its own slide; both are answered by the slides around them. The deck carries no patient cases.
stem: Why estrogen-only preparations aren’t used as contraceptives?

options.html: They are not reliably absorbed when taken by the oral route
They are the preparations most strongly linked to breast cancer
They have no effect on cervical mucus or on tubal peristalsis
They leave the endometrium under unopposed proliferative drive

answer:
The correct answer is D. The deck poses this as a full-slide question immediately after the slide showing that estrogens and progestins have opposing effects on the endometrium: estrogen drives proliferation and differentiation and so raises the risk of endometrial cancer, while a progestin opposes that proliferation and is protective. An estrogen given alone leaves that proliferation unopposed, which is why a progestin is added — in contraception and, for a woman with an intact uterus, in hormone replacement therapy too.

A is wrong: ethinyl estradiol is given orally at 10–50 mcg and is well absorbed, though it does undergo hepatic metabolism and enterohepatic recirculation. C describes the local actions of a progestin, not a reason estrogen alone fails. B is the trap: estrogen and progestin are synergic on breast tissue, both driving proliferation, so a combined preparation is not the safer one on that axis — the breast is the one risk that adding a progestin does not fix.

The slide poses the question and does not print options; the four here are written from this deck’s own slides, and the stem is copied verbatim, unpunctuated as the deck has it.

lectureMeta: Case from Contraception 2026.pdf slides 58-63. Keyed from the deck's Case Points slides.
stem: Clarise is an 18 yo G0, recently sexually active. She has been using condoms until now with a monogamous male partner. She is interested in birth control options. Her family history is significant for her mother who developed a deep vein thrombosis (DVT) after a surgery, and her sister who developed a pulmonary embolus (PE) after starting a birth control pill. She is afraid of weight gain, and wants to know what her best options might be?

options.html: A combined oral contraceptive, since her own thrombotic history is negative
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, since it avoids estrogen altogether
A progestin-only pill, a copper IUD, or a levonorgestrel intrauterine system
A combined transdermal patch, since it avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism entirely

answer:
C. Two separate features of her story each rule out an option, and what is left is the answer.

The family history is the estrogen question. A first-degree relative with a post-operative DVT and a sister who developed a PE after starting a birth control pill is the pattern that raises a hereditary thrombophilia such as Factor V Leiden. The deck's own point is that ⭐ estrogens should likely be avoided until she is tested - which disposes of A and D. D is the specific trap: the patch avoids first-pass metabolism, but that is not protective, and the combined methods that bypass first pass carry a higher thromboembolic risk, not a lower one.

The weight-gain concern is the Depo question. ⭐ Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate is the only contraceptive known to cause weight gain - an average of 7 lb in the first year, with early gain predicting ongoing gain. She has raised weight gain unprompted, so B is the one progestin-only method to steer away from.

That leaves the deck's own list: the progestin-only pill, the copper IUD and the levonorgestrel intrauterine system are all valid.

Principle: a family history of estrogen-associated VTE removes estrogen until proven otherwise; after that, pick the progestin-only method by the side effect the patient actually cares about.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lectureMeta: Case from Contraception 2026.pdf slides 58-63. Keyed from the deck's Case Points slides.
stem: Beth is a 41 year old G2P2 who has completed child bearing. She has regular menses that are fairly light. She is a non-smoker, and is tired of taking a birth control pill every day. She has no drug coverage and finds the monthly costs of birth control difficult to manage, and often goes 2-3 months at a time with no birth control because of this. What cost effective methods of birth control can be offered in this setting?

options.html: A copper intrauterine device, or permanent contraception covered by OHIP
A levonorgestrel intrauterine system, the cheapest long-acting option here
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, injected every twelve to thirteen weeks
A continuous combined oral contraceptive to skip the withdrawal bleed

answer:
A. The clinical problem in this stem is not contraceptive efficacy - it is that ⭐ cost is causing 2-3 month gaps with no contraception at all, which is the actual pregnancy risk. So the question is which method removes the recurring cost.

  • The copper IUD is cheap up front, generally $30-75, and then costs nothing for 3-10 years. Her periods are already light and regular, which matters because the copper IUD's main drawback is that it can ↑ menstrual blood loss and dysmenorrhea - she has headroom for that.
  • Permanent contraception is the deck's second answer, and it fits because she has completed childbearing and it is covered by OHIP. The trade is surgery, which the copper IUD avoids.

B is wrong on the stated ground: the LNG-IUS is an excellent method but it is not the cheap one - the copper device is. C keeps a recurring cost and a clinic visit every 12-13 weeks, which is the pattern she is already failing. D leaves her taking a pill every day, which she has told you she is tired of, and leaves the monthly cost in place.

Principle: when non-adherence is driven by cost, the fix is a method with no recurring cost, not a more effective method she still cannot afford.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lectureMeta: Case from Contraception 2026.pdf slides 58-63. Keyed from the deck's Case Points slides.
stem: Tara is a 36 yo G6T1P1A4L1 who presents for a discussion about birth control options to the sexual health clinic. Her gynecologic history is significant for PID (pelvic inflammatory disease) 2 years ago. She has very heavy but predictable periods. She smokes 1 pack/day and admits to daily cannabis use as well as IV drug use. She is Hep C and HIV positive, and is not compliant with her medications. She is currently homeless, and is being trafficked, admitting to prostitution to afford her drug use. She does not want to become pregnant at this time. What contraceptive options are contraindicated?

options.html: All estrogen-containing methods, because she smokes and is over 35 years old
Any intrauterine device, because of her pelvic inflammatory disease two years ago
All progestin-only methods, because hepatitis C impairs their hepatic clearance
Any long-acting method, because she is unlikely to return to have it removed

answer:
A. ⭐ Smoking more than 15 cigarettes a day over the age of 35 is an absolute contraindication to combined hormonal contraception - she smokes a pack a day and is 36. That rules out the pill, the patch and the ring.

B is the trap, and the deck flags it explicitly: "There are NO contraindications to insertion of an IUD on the previous slide." Read the absolute contraindications to intrauterine contraception and notice what is not on the list - smoking, age, HIV, nulliparity, and ⭐ a past PID. Only current PID or cervicitis contraindicates an IUD. Her PID was two years ago.

C is invented - hepatic clearance is not how progestin-only methods are contraindicated, and none of her liver disease rules them out. D confuses a practical concern with a contraindication; being hard to follow up is an argument for a long-acting method, not against one.

Principle: the list of absolute IUD contraindications is short, and most of what patients like Tara are refused on is not on it.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lectureMeta: Case from Contraception 2026.pdf slides 58-63. Keyed from the deck's Case Points slides.
stem: Tara is a 36 yo G6T1P1A4L1 who presents for a discussion about birth control options to the sexual health clinic. Her gynecologic history is significant for PID (pelvic inflammatory disease) 2 years ago. She has very heavy but predictable periods. She smokes 1 pack/day and admits to daily cannabis use as well as IV drug use. She is Hep C and HIV positive, and is not compliant with her medications. She is currently homeless, and is being trafficked, admitting to prostitution to afford her drug use. She does not want to become pregnant at this time. What contraceptive option might be best for her?

options.html: A progestin-only pill, which she can start today with no procedure required
A compassionate levonorgestrel intrauterine system, inserted the same day
Condoms alone, which also protect her partners from HIV and hepatitis C
A combined oral contraceptive, once her smoking has been addressed in clinic

answer:
B. Three facts in the stem point the same way.

  1. ⭐ She is non-compliant with her other medications, so anything requiring daily action will fail. That removes A and D on adherence grounds before the pharmacology is even considered - and D is separately contraindicated (see Q3).
  2. ⭐ She is at very high risk of unintended pregnancy, so a LARC is preferred - the LNG-IUS and the implant are the two methods whose 12-month continuation runs in the 83-88% band while everything else sits at 49-57%.
  3. Her periods are very heavy, and the LNG-IUS treats that as well as preventing pregnancy.

The word compassionate is doing real work: cost is a barrier, and the deck's point is that the device cost is the obstacle to overcome, not the choice of device. The deck adds a practical step - ⭐ consider prophylactic STI treatment and insert the same day after a negative pregnancy test, rather than sending her away to come back.

C is not wrong about STI protection, but condoms have a typical-use failure of 18% and depend on partner cooperation she may not have; as her sole method they do not meet her stated goal.

Principle: where follow-up is unlikely, the best method is the one that works after she walks out of the room today.

lectureMeta: Case from STI2021Slides.pdf / AcutePelvicPain_2021.pdf. Keyed.
stem: Katie is a 25 y.o. presenting to the ER with sudden onset of RLQ pain and vaginal bleeding. She is sexually active and using condoms as her method of contraception. She also describes pain in her shoulders and feeling lightheaded. She endorses tenesmus. Her B-HCG is 2345, her Hb is 82. What is her diagnosis?

options.html: Acute pelvic inflammatory disease with a tubo-ovarian abscess
A ruptured haemorrhagic ovarian cyst occurring at mid-cycle
An incomplete spontaneous abortion at around eight weeks
A ruptured ectopic pregnancy with blood in the peritoneum

answer:
D. The positive β-hCG of 2345 and the Hb of 82 are the two numbers that close this.

  • β-hCG 2345 is above the discriminatory zone. ⭐ At a β-hCG over 1500 an intrauterine pregnancy should be visible on transvaginal ultrasound. A pregnancy that is not where it should be, at a level where it would be seen, is ectopic until proven otherwise.
  • The shoulder pain and the tenesmus are both rupture signs, not ectopic signs. ⭐ Shoulder-tip pain comes from blood irritating the diaphragm, and tenesmus from blood pooling in the pelvis. Together with lightheadedness and an Hb of 82, she has bled into her abdomen.

A does not fit: PID does not raise β-hCG, and her pain is sudden and lateralized rather than generalized. B is the closest mimic and can present identically - shoulder pain, tenesmus, hypotension - but ⭐ a ruptured cyst has a NEGATIVE β-hCG, which is exactly what rules it out here. C would explain bleeding and a positive β-hCG but not the shoulder pain, the tenesmus or the haemoglobin.

Principle: in a reproductive-age woman with pain and bleeding, the β-hCG sorts the differential in one step, and the discriminatory zone tells you what the ultrasound should have shown.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lectureMeta: Case from STI2021Slides.pdf / AcutePelvicPain_2021.pdf. Keyed.
stem: Sara is a 17 y.o. presenting for a routine gynecologic exam. She reports feeling generally unwell; fevers, chills, nausea. She also complains of generalized pelvic pain and pain with intercourse. Lately she has noticed a foul smelling vaginal discharge. Her WBC is 22, her B-HCG is negative. She has the "chandelier" sign on physical exam. What is her diagnosis?

options.html: An ovarian torsion with secondary inflammatory change
Acute pelvic inflammatory disease of the genital tract
A ruptured ectopic pregnancy with peritoneal irritation
Bacterial vaginosis with secondary candidal vulvitis

answer:
B. The "chandelier sign" is cervical motion tenderness - so named because the patient comes off the table - and in this context it is close to diagnostic.

Everything else assembles around it: fever and chills, a WBC of 22, generalized pelvic pain rather than lateralized, dyspareunia, and a foul-smelling discharge in a sexually active 17-year-old. ⭐ Sexually active youth under 25 is itself a listed STI risk factor, and chlamydia and gonorrhea are the two organisms most commonly associated with PID.

C is excluded by the negative β-hCG. A would give sudden, severe, lateralized pain rather than a generalized ache with fever, and would not produce discharge. D explains the discharge and nothing else - bacterial vaginosis does not cause fever, a WBC of 22, or cervical motion tenderness; it is a lower-tract problem and this is an upper-tract one.

⭐ Her age is also an admission criterion. Youth and adolescence is on the list of indications for hospitalization, alongside failure of oral therapy, severe illness, tubo-ovarian abscess, immunodeficiency and pregnancy.

Principle: cervical motion tenderness plus fever in a sexually active patient with a negative β-hCG is PID until proven otherwise.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lecture: Clinical Approach to Acute Pelvic Pain
lectureMeta: Case from AcutePelvicPain_2021.pdf. Keyed.
stem: Helen is a 45 y.o G3P3 presenting to the ER with acute onset of LLQ pain. She describes being stopped in the middle of her golf game with a sharp stabbing pain radiating to her back. She vomited once and collapsed. Her HR is 110, her temp is 37.5, her BhCG is <1, her Hgb is 128 and stable. On pelvic exam there is a 9cm mass palpable and tender; what is her diagnosis?

options.html: A degenerating pedunculated uterine fibroid causing pain
Diverticulitis of the sigmoid colon with a phlegmon
Ovarian torsion around its ligamentous supports
A ruptured ectopic pregnancy with hypovolaemia

answer:
C. Three features converge.

  1. ⭐ It began during vigorous activity. The deck names golf specifically, alongside intercourse and vigorous exercise.
  2. ⭐ There is a 9 cm mass. This is the mechanism: a normal ovary can tort, but enlarged ovaries are far more likely to, acting like a weighted pendulum. The mass is not an incidental finding, it is the cause.
  3. The haemoglobin is 128 and stable. She is tachycardic from pain, not from bleeding - which separates this from every haemorrhagic diagnosis on the list.

D is excluded by the β-hCG of < 1. B could give LLQ pain but not sudden onset mid-swing, and would be expected to run a fever. A is the best distractor, since a pedunculated fibroid can also tort - but the palpable mass here is adnexal and the presentation is the classic ovarian one.

⭐ This is a surgical emergency to preserve the ovary. The mechanism is worth holding: compression of the infundibulopelvic ligament ↓ venous outflow while arterial perfusion continues, so the ovary becomes oedematous and enlarges, which compresses the vessels further - and then ischaemia, necrosis and infarction. Afterwards, ⭐ investigate the underlying mass, benign versus malignant.

Principle: sudden lateralized pain after exertion with an adnexal mass and a normal haemoglobin is torsion, and the clock is on the ovary.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lecture: Clinical Approach to Acute Pelvic Pain
lectureMeta: Case from AcutePelvicPain_2021.pdf. Keyed.
stem: Lisa is a 33 year old nulligravid woman who has been trying to conceive. She presents to the emergency room with 9/10 pain in the right lower quadrant. She endorses tenesmus, shoulder pain when she lays down, and lightheadedness when standing. The pain presented suddenly after intercourse. Her last menstrual period was just over 2 weeks ago. Her BhCG is <1. Her Hgb is 78, dropping from 110 at presentation a few hours earlier. Her BP is 110/70 HR 80 laying flat, but 86/55 standing with a HR of 112. What is her diagnosis?

options.html: A ruptured ovarian cyst with haemorrhage into the peritoneum
A ruptured ectopic pregnancy in the right fallopian tube
Ovarian torsion with early infarction of the right ovary and tube
Acute pelvic inflammatory disease with a pelvic abscess

answer:
A. This is Katie's presentation with one number changed, and that number decides it.

⭐ Her β-hCG is < 1. Everything else - tenesmus, shoulder pain lying down, a haemoglobin falling from 110 to 78, and postural hypotension (110/70 lying, 86/55 standing with a HR of 112) - says she is bleeding into her abdomen. But she is not pregnant, so B is impossible.

The timing and trigger fit a cyst exactly: ⭐ ruptured cysts occur around ovulation, 2-3 weeks from the last menstrual period, which is precisely where she is, and ⭐ they may rupture secondary to blunt trauma such as intercourse, which is what happened.

C does not bleed like this - torsion causes ischaemia, not haemoperitoneum, and would not drop her haemoglobin by 32 in a few hours. D is excluded by the sudden onset, the absence of fever and discharge, and the falling haemoglobin.

⭐ A rupture with this much bleeding is relatively uncommon - most often the bleeding is minimal or absent, which is why her instability is the notable feature. Management is usually expectant, but ongoing bleeding or haemodynamic instability means surgery, and ⭐ recurrence is prevented with ovulatory suppression - which is a live problem here, because she is trying to conceive.

Principle: pain, shoulder tip pain and a falling haemoglobin say haemoperitoneum; the β-hCG says which organ it came from.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lecture: Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain
lectureMeta: Case from ChronicPelvicPain_2021.pdf slides 8-43. Keyed.
stem: Jessica is a 19 y.o G0 with painful menses. She describes regular cycles every 29 days lasting 7 days. During the first 2 days she experiences heavier flow with severe cramps radiating to her back. The pain lessens as her cycle goes on. What does she have?

options.html: Endometriosis with deep infiltrating rectovaginal disease
Adenomyosis presenting early in the reproductive years
Myofascial pelvic pain from raised pelvic floor resting tone
Primary dysmenorrhoea, which is a clinical diagnosis

answer:
D. Two features of the timing make this primary rather than secondary.

  1. ⭐ The pain occurs with menses, not before it. It is worst on the first two days and eases as the cycle goes on. Endometriosis characteristically begins about two days before the bleeding starts.
  2. ⭐ She is 19. Primary dysmenorrhoea belongs to the late teens and twenties and then declines; secondary dysmenorrhoea becomes more common with aging. The age direction is the discriminator.

The mechanism explains the description. Menses is a generalized inflammatory state: prostaglandins from endometrial sloughing induce contractions; ⭐ when uterine pressure exceeds arterial pressure the uterus becomes ischaemic; anaerobic metabolites accumulate and stimulate type C pain neurons. That is why the pain is cramping, why it tracks the heaviest flow, and why an NSAID is first line.

⭐ There are no laboratory abnormalities and no abnormal physical findings in dysmenorrhoea - which is what makes A, B and C unattractive here, since each would be expected to leave something on examination. B is additionally wrong on demographics: adenomyosis presents in the 4th and 5th decades, in parous women, and she is a 19-year-old G0.

Principle: pain with menses in a teenager is primary; pain that starts before menses, or starts later in life, is secondary and needs a structural explanation.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lecture: Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain
lectureMeta: Case from ChronicPelvicPain_2021.pdf slides 8-43. Keyed.
stem: Jessica is now 25. She has noticed her painful periods have gotten much worse, in fact the pain begins 2 days prior to the onset of menses. She is unable to leave the house for the first 24 hours due to severe pain. It now radiates down her left leg. She has also noticed new onset of deep dyspareunia. What do you suspect?

options.html: Primary dysmenorrhoea that has worsened with age
Endometriosis, with implants outside the uterine cavity
Adenomyosis, with endometrium within the myometrium
A degenerating submucosal fibroid distorting the uterine cavity

answer:
B. She is the same patient as Q9, and three things have changed.

  1. ⭐ The pain now begins two days BEFORE menses. That shift, from pain with bleeding to pain preceding it, is the single most useful change in the stem.
  2. It radiates down her leg, which is the pattern of disease outside the uterus rather than within it.
  3. ⭐ New deep dyspareunia. Deep pain points to endometriosis, masses, adhesions or musculoskeletal causes; superficial pain on penetration points instead to vulvodynia, atrophy, vulvar skin conditions or vaginismus.

A is excluded by that change in timing - primary dysmenorrhoea does not migrate earlier in the cycle, and it declines rather than worsens through the twenties. C is wrong on demographics again: adenomyosis is a disease of parous women in their 40s and 50s, and she is a nulligravid 25-year-old. D would be expected to cause abnormal bleeding rather than this pain pattern, and she reports none.

⚠ ⭐ Expect the examination to be normal. The findings that may appear - nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments, a fixed immobile uterus, an endometrioma - are listed by the deck alongside "often NOTHING". And ⭐ the severity of disease does not correlate with the degree of pain, so a normal-looking pelvis does not mean mild disease.

Principle: pain that moves to before the period, radiates, and brings deep dyspareunia is endometriosis, and a normal examination does not argue against it.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lecture: Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain
lectureMeta: Case from ChronicPelvicPain_2021.pdf slides 8-43. Keyed.
stem: Jessica underwent laparoscopy and ablation of endometriotic implants. She went on to have 3 successful pregnancies. Now at 42, she notices her periods are less painful then before, but much heavier. Despite being on continuous OCP's she often bleeds through her clothing at work. She also notes a heavy pelvic sensation. She has no hot flashes or night sweats. What does she likely have?

options.html: Recurrent endometriosis after her earlier ablation
Adenomyosis, with endometrium in the myometrium

answer:
C. The deck is deliberately testing whether the earlier diagnosis anchors you. Read what has changed: ⭐ her periods are LESS painful than before but much HEAVIER. Endometriosis does not behave that way.

Adenomyosis fits on every axis:

  • ⭐ She is now parous and in her 5th decade - the deck puts adenomyosis in the 4th and 5th decades and in parous women, and notes it is uncommon in nulligravids
  • Menorrhagia is its dominant symptom, with dysmenorrhea only sometimes
  • The heavy pelvic sensation reflects an enlarged uterus - the myometrium undergoes smooth muscle hypertrophy, which is what actually enlarges it

The mechanism explains both symptoms at once: ⭐ more endometrial tissue plus entrapped blood in cystic areas that rupture gives the bleeding, and ⭐ the myometrium contracting because blood is irritating it gives the pain.

A is excluded by the pain getting better. D is a reasonable thought at 42, but ⭐ she has no hot flashes or night sweats, and the deck includes that line to close it off. B is less likely on continuous OCP, which opposes the endometrium rather than leaving it unopposed.

⭐ Expect a tender, enlarged, boggy uterus - "boggy" is the word that separates it from the firm, irregular uterus of fibroids. And note that ⭐ the diagnosis cannot be made by biopsy, because the glands are too deep; it is largely clinical, and is often found incidentally at the hysterectomy of a woman who failed medical management.

Principle: when the pain improves and the bleeding worsens in a parous woman in her forties, stop thinking about the old diagnosis.

lecture: Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain
lectureMeta: Case from ChronicPelvicPain_2021.pdf slides 8-43. Keyed.
stem: Jessica's sister, Erica comes to see you after hearing about what good care you provided her sister. She is 35 and wishing to achieve a pregnancy. Lately she has noticed increasingly heavy periods and a larger than usual abdominal girth. Her B-HCG is negative. On exam you note an approx. 20 week size, mobile uterus. What is the likely diagnosis?

options.html: Uterine fibroids, which are benign smooth muscle tumours
Adenomyosis producing a diffusely enlarged and boggy uterus
An ovarian malignancy with an associated pelvic mass
A molar pregnancy with a uterus large for its dates

answer:
A. Two words in the examination finding decide this: 20 week size and ⭐ mobile.

  • The size. A uterus enlarged to 20 weeks in a non-pregnant 35-year-old is a mass lesion, and fibroids are ⭐ the most common neoplasm in females, clinically apparent in 25% of reproductive-age women and present on imaging in about 50% of women over 40.
  • The mobility. A mobile uterus argues against the adhesions and fixation of malignancy or advanced endometriosis.
  • The bleeding. ⭐ Abnormal uterine bleeding is the commonest symptom of fibroids, and is seen most with submucosal ones, which sit against the cavity.

D is excluded by the negative β-hCG. C would not typically present as a uniformly enlarged, mobile uterus. B is the real distractor, and it is wrong on scale: adenomyosis produces a diffusely enlarged, boggy uterus, not a 20-week irregular one.

⭐ Her wish to conceive changes the management, not the diagnosis. Fibroids cause reproductive dysfunction only when they distort the uterine cavity, so where they sit matters more than how many there are. And it rules an option out: ⭐ pregnancy after uterine artery embolization is NOT advised - the evidence is case reports only - so myomectomy is the fertility-sparing route.

Principle: an enlarged, mobile, non-pregnant uterus with heavy periods is fibroids; the fertility question then decides between myomectomy and everything else.
