lecture: Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain
lectureMeta: Case from ChronicPelvicPain_2021.pdf slides 8-43. Keyed.
stem: Mya is a 23 y.o nulliparous woman presenting with pelvic pain for the past 5 years. It is not associated with any time in her cycle. She describes it as generalized, debilitating pain that prevents her from working or attending school. Her cycles are regular. She is not sexually active due to the pain. On physical exam she has a globally tender pelvis; midline mobile uterus with no adnexal masses. Speculum exam was not carried out due to extreme pain. What is her diagnosis?

options.html: Endometriosis with deeply infiltrating pelvic implants
Interstitial cystitis, also called painful bladder syndrome
Chronic pelvic inflammatory disease with dense adhesions
Myofascial pelvic pain from raised pelvic floor tone

answer:
D. ⭐ The pain is not associated with any time in her cycle. That single feature moves the differential out of gynaecology - if there is no cyclic component, extra-gynaecologic causes must be considered, and a thorough review of systems is what sorts them.

The examination then confirms it. A globally tender pelvis with a midline, mobile uterus and no adnexal masses is a muscular finding, not a structural one - there is nothing to feel because the problem is tone rather than tissue. Myofascial pelvic pain involves ⭐ a high resting tone in the muscles and fascia attaching to the bony pelvis, and the deck names levator ani and piriformis.

A and C both require something to find, and she has a normal uterus and no masses. A is further undermined by the absence of any cyclic pattern, since endometrial implants respond to the cycle. B is a genuine differential for chronic pelvic pain, but nothing in the stem points at the bladder.

⭐ Note who these patients tend to be: many have a history of sexual abuse, poor sexual experience, recurrent infection (yeast, UTI, PID) or endometriosis - and ⭐ up to 50% of women with chronic pelvic pain have experienced some kind of abuse or trauma. Treatment is deliberately multidisciplinary, manual soft tissue release is essential, and ⚠ ⭐ the goal is pain reduction and improved function, not cure.

Principle: pain with no cyclic pattern and a normal structural examination is muscular until proven otherwise.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lecture: Approach to Pathology of AUB & Pelvic Pain
lectureMeta: Case from Weir_AUBPain_slides.pdf. Keyed except Q16, which the deck poses no question for.
stem: Alexa is a 40 year old female with bleeding between periods and daily spotting. Her cycles are 27 days with 7 days of bleeding, she is on no medications and has no other bleeding. Her BP is 122/80, HR 75, RR 15, temp 37.5. Her exam is normal except for a small fleshy 2 cm cervical mass. For Alexa what are the possible causes of AUB?

options.html: The full ABCDEHIN differential, since nothing has yet narrowed it
The structural causes only, since a mass is visible at the cervical os
Dysfunctional uterine bleeding, given her otherwise regular cycles
A coagulopathy, since intermenstrual spotting can suggest von Willebrand disease

answer:
B. ⭐ A visible mass at the os is what narrows the differential, and that is the whole method this lecture is teaching: use age, common reasons and clues to cut a long list down.

The differential for AUB is ABCDEHIN, and it divides into two halves:

  • Structural - Anatomic, Baby, Neoplasia
  • Functional - Coagulopathy, DUB, Endocrine, Hormones, Infectious

A fleshy 2 cm mass protruding at the cervical os is a structural finding, so the three starred letters are where the answer lives. Within A, the benign uterine lesions are PALE - Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Endometritis - and ⭐ the polyp and the leiomyoma are the two that can present at the os, which is why they are the leading candidates here, alongside malignancy.

A is true of a 40-year-old before you examine her, which is exactly the point - the deck shows the full list first and then strikes it down. C is wrong twice over: her cycles are regular, and ⭐ DUB is a diagnosis of exclusion, so it cannot be reached while a visible lesion is unexplained. D is not supported - there is no other bleeding, no medication history and no bruising.

⭐ Whatever it is, remove it and send the ENTIRE specimen to pathology. A polyp is rarely malignant, but rarely is not never.

Principle: examine before you differential-diagnose; one visible finding can delete five of the eight letters.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lecture: Approach to Pathology of AUB & Pelvic Pain
lectureMeta: Case from Weir_AUBPain_slides.pdf. Keyed except Q16, which the deck poses no question for.
stem: For Alexa what are the possible causes of AUB if there was NO lesion at cervix and she had severe dysmenorrhea?

options.html: Neoplasia, since a 40 year old with pain requires urgent endometrial sampling
Baby, since a pregnancy complication explains both bleeding and cramping pain
Secondary dysmenorrhoea, from the PALE lesions or from endometriosis
Primary dysmenorrhoea, which is the commonest cause of painful periods

answer:
C. Removing the cervical mass removes the structural shortcut, but adding severe dysmenorrhoea opens a second differential - and the same age-based logic applies to the pain as to the bleeding.

Primary (functional)Secondary (structural, acquired)
Whoyounger - late teens and 20s, then declines⭐ more common with aging
WhatDUB in the reproductive years⭐ PALE + endometriosis

⭐ Alexa is 40, and the age direction is the discriminator: dysmenorrhoea that starts or worsens with age is structural until proven otherwise. That is what makes D the trap - primary dysmenorrhoea is indeed common, but it declines through the twenties and does not newly appear at 40.

So the candidates are the PALE lesions - polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, endometritis - plus endometriosis. ⭐ Remember that the E in PALE is endometritis, not endometriosis; endometriosis is a separate entry on the secondary-dysmenorrhoea list, which is why the deck prints the reminder.

A overreaches - neoplasia stays on the list at 40, but it is not the answer to "what are the possible causes". B is not supported by anything in the stem, though a β-hCG remains part of the workup regardless.

Principle: the same question - how old is she, and is this new? - sorts the bleeding and the pain.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lecture: Approach to Pathology of AUB & Pelvic Pain
lectureMeta: Case from Weir_AUBPain_slides.pdf. Keyed except Q16, which the deck poses no question for.
stem: Adele is a 35 year old female who has been trying to get pregnant for 1 year, with no AUB. She has new worsening painful periods and pelvic pain prior to the onset of her period. Her BP is 120/75, HR 79, RR 13, temp 37.6. On examination the pelvic exam is painful, there are nodules in the rectovaginal septum, and the uterus is fixed. Investigations: lab medicine, imaging, pathology.

options.html: Endometrial glands and stroma with hemosiderin, outside the uterus
Endometrial glands and stroma deep within the uterine myometrium
A well circumscribed nodule made of bundles of smooth muscle cells
Endometrial glands and stroma with dilated glands, on a fibrous stalk

answer:
A. The examination has already made the diagnosis: ⭐ nodularity in the rectovaginal septum plus a fixed uterus is endometriosis, and the deck's laparoscopy image shows pigmented "powder burns".

The histology is the point of the question. ⭐ The pathologist needs any TWO of three features:

  1. endometrial epithelium / glands
  2. endometrial stroma
  3. hemosiderin

Hemosiderin is the brown iron pigment left by repeated bleeding, and its presence outside the uterus is what distinguishes this from every other option. ⚠ ⭐ Late disease "burns out" - the endometrial tissue disappears and only fibrosis remains - so a negative biopsy in longstanding disease does not exclude it.

B describes adenomyosis, which is the same tissue in the wrong place within the myometrium - and which ⭐ cannot be diagnosed by biopsy at all, because the glands are too deep. C describes a leiomyoma. D describes an endometrial polyp, whose dilated glands and stalk sit inside the cavity.

⭐ Her infertility is expected. Endometriosis affects 30-40% of these patients with infertility, and the deck's own check asks which lesions from this session associate with infertility: endometriosis, endometrial polyp and leiomyoma - but NOT adenomyosis.

Principle: the same four tissues are told apart by where they are, and endometriosis is the one that brings hemosiderin with it.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lecture: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
lectureMeta: Case from Repro-invasive testing 2023.pdf slides 17-23. Keyed.
stem: Doris is a 29 year old woman. Fetal anatomic scan at 18 weeks reveals an omphalocele and bilateral cleft lip and palate. What are the diagnostic options available?

options.html: Chorionic villus sampling, which samples placental tissue directly
NIPT alone, since its detection rate for the trisomies exceeds 99%
A repeat detailed anatomy ultrasound at 22 weeks for confirmation
Amniocentesis, with NIPT available as a screening test beforehand

answer:
D. ⭐ Multiple midline defects and congenital anomalies should make you think chromosomal aneuploidy, and with an omphalocele plus bilateral cleft lip and palate the most likely is trisomy 13.

The question asks for diagnostic options, and the distinction between screening and diagnosis is the whole point:

  • NIPT is a SCREEN. It assesses cell-free fetal DNA in maternal serum, and ⭐ a screen-positive NIPT still needs definitive testing.
  • Amniocentesis is DIAGNOSTIC, and at 18 weeks she is inside its 15-20 week window.

A is wrong on timing: ⭐ chorionic villus sampling is an 11-13 week test and that window has closed. C adds nothing diagnostic - imaging describes the anomalies, it does not karyotype them. B confuses a screen with a diagnosis, and ⭐ Ontario does not recommend NIPT as a first-line screen for low-risk women in any case.

⚠ ⭐ The clock is the real constraint. NIPT takes about 10 days, a CVS microarray about 2 weeks, and a single-gene test 3 weeks minimum - against a 24-week limit on termination. She is already 18 weeks. Doing the screen first and then the diagnostic test may leave no room for a decision, which is why the honest question to ask the couple is whether they want to know definitively and whether it would change management.

Principle: work backwards from 24 weeks, and do not spend a fortnight on a screen when the answer will need a diagnostic test anyway.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lecture: Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada
lectureMeta: Case from Repro-invasive testing 2023.pdf slides 17-23. Keyed.
stem: The result is 46, XX, t(13;21)(q10;q10),+13. Doris and Jeff have their chromosomes checked, and two weeks later Doris is found to have a 45, XX, der(13;21)(q10;q10) karyotype. What are the implications for this family?

options.html: None beyond this pregnancy, since the translocation arose de novo in the fetus
An increased risk of unbalanced translocations in her future pregnancies
Her siblings are unaffected, since a balanced carrier has a normal phenotype
A 25% recurrence risk, as for any autosomal recessive condition in a family

answer:
B. Doris carries a balanced Robertsonian translocation - 45 chromosomes, with 13 and 21 joined. She is healthy because she has the normal amount of genetic material; it is simply arranged differently. Her fetus inherited an unbalanced version and so has an extra 13.

⭐ That is a permanent, heritable risk, not a one-off event, and it reaches beyond this pregnancy in four directions:

  • increased risk of unbalanced translocations in future pregnancies
  • the option of prenatal diagnosis in those pregnancies
  • the option of preimplantation genetic diagnosis
  • ⭐ a daughter has a 50% chance of being a carrier

⭐ And her siblings may also be carriers - they need genetic counselling and should be offered testing. That is what makes C wrong: a balanced carrier's phenotype is normal, which is precisely why the relatives do not know and have to be told. A is excluded by the maternal karyotype, which is the reason both parents were tested. D applies the wrong inheritance model - a translocation is not a recessive allele.

⭐ One fetal diagnosis has just generated referrals for an entire extended family, and that cascade is the examinable idea.

Principle: when a fetal aneuploidy turns out to be translocation-derived, karyotype the parents - the result changes the counselling for everyone related to the carrier.

stem: 36 year old with A very itchy rash. Her symptoms flare with heat and friction. The rash does not respond to topical steroid, She scratches all the time and keeps her husband up at night. She has hayfever and environmental allergies. Your Diagnosis Is?
answer:
B. The three-lichen table sorts this in one row: ⭐ LSC is the one with ++++ ITCH and NO scarring, while both LS and LP itch or burn and both scar.

Everything in the stem is the itch cycle. Lichen simplex chronicus is ⭐ the end stage of itch → scratch → itch, it is worse with heat, humidity, stress and irritation - she flares with heat and friction - and the scratching is continuous enough to keep her husband awake, which is the deck's own detail.

Her atopy is the clue to the underlying cause. ⭐ LSC is a reaction, not a diagnosis in itself, and atopic dermatitis is on the list of dermatoses that start it, alongside psoriasis, LS, LP and contact dermatitis. So C is not so much wrong as incomplete - contact dermatitis is one of the things that causes LSC.

A and D both scar, and neither is described. Note also that the rash does not respond to topical steroid - which in LSC means the cycle has not been broken, and the treatment is a superpotent steroid on a taper plus ⭐ night sedation (doxepin or hydroxyzine), because the damage is done in sleep.

Principle: maximal itch with no scarring is LSC - then go looking for what started the itch.

stem: 60 year old presents for her routine pap smear. She has hypothyroidism but is otherwise healthy. On examination you see classic white or waxy papules and plaques, diffuse erythema, a cellophane-like surface sheen that is crinkled and atrophic, in a figure of eight pattern. Your Diagnosis Is?
answer:
A. Three features are close to pathognomonic, and the deck lists all three in its speaker notes: ⭐ a cellophane-like surface sheen, crinkled and atrophic, ⭐ the figure-of-eight / hourglass pattern, and the classic white or waxy papules and plaques.

Her hypothyroidism is not incidental. ⭐ Lichen sclerosus is associated with hypothyroidism, and the deck puts it in the stem for that reason. Her age fits too - LS is classically perimenopausal, 40-50 years, and it is ⭐ the commonest cause of chronic vulvar disease at a prevalence of 1/300 to 1/1000.

⚠ ⭐ She is asymptomatic, and that does not argue against it. Itch occurs in 90% and pain or burning in 40%, but asymptomatic presentation is on the list - and the deck's note is that ⭐ asymptomatic vulvar scarring should make you look for LS.

D is the hardest distractor because hypertrophic LP looks like LS - the separator is that ⭐ LP involves the vagina and the mouth and LS does not, so examine all three. B is excluded by the atrophy and scarring, which LSC does not produce. C would not give this morphology.

⭐ The reason this matters is cancer. About 4% develop squamous cell carcinoma, in longstanding (> 7 years) and poorly controlled disease - which is why the treatment instruction is maintenance clobetasol 1-3x weekly and TREAT FOREVER, not a course of steroid for a rash.

Principle: white, crinkled, figure-of-eight, and a thyroid history - and then treat it indefinitely, because it is premalignant.

stem: 50 year old presents with dyspareunia. She is otherwise healthy. Your Diagnosis Is?
answer:
D. Lichen planus is the lichen that presents with pain rather than itch - ⭐ 70-75% painful versus 60% itchy - and dyspareunia is named first among its painful presentations, alongside dysuria and apareunia. Her age fits: LP is a disease of older women, 50s-60s.

The form that causes dyspareunia is the erosive one, which is ⭐ the most common genital pattern in women: red plaques with whitish, lacy edges, glazed erythema, erosions, ulcers and scarring. Eroded mucosa hurts with contact, which is the mechanism.

⭐ The instruction that follows is the examinable part: ALWAYS examine the vulva, the vagina AND the mouth. LP is the only one of the three lichens that goes into the vagina and the mouth - and ⚠ the vulva can look normal while the vagina is actively involved, so a normal vulvar examination does not end the search.

A presents at a similar age but with itch and the characteristic white crinkled sheen. B would be dominated by itch and would not scar. C does not produce this picture.

⭐ Treatment includes something the other two do not need: DILATORS, plus vaginal hydrocortisone suppositories - because the scarring is inside the vagina and will close it. And like LS, it carries a malignant risk: 2-3% progress to squamous cell carcinoma.

Principle: pain rather than itch, at 50, is lichen planus - and the examination is not finished until you have looked in her mouth.

stem: 17 yo with this vulvar lesion. It is the third time this has happened many years apart. All episodes have been a day or two after she had strep throat. Not painful initially then becomes uncomfortable. The lesion is small like 3 mm in diameter, dark almost black, not raised in fact slightly depressed. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Primary genital herpes simplex virus infection
A vulvar melanoma arising in an area of melanosis
An aphthous ulcer, before it has fully ulcerated

answer:
C. ⭐ Aphthae classically occur after a viral syndrome, in girls between roughly 9 and 20 - and every element of this stem is that description.

  • The trigger: each of the three episodes followed strep throat by a day or two
  • The pattern: recurrent, many years apart, rather than clustered
  • The lesion: 3 mm, dark, slightly depressed rather than raised - which is the deck's point that this is an early presentation before it ulcerates, and the reason it does not yet look like an ulcer
  • The pain: not painful initially, becoming uncomfortable

⭐ These patients also get oral aphthae, but usually not at the same time, so asking about mouth ulcers is useful even when the mouth is currently clear. In severe cases ⚠ the pain can be bad enough that the patient cannot urinate.

A is the deck's own stated alternative - ⭐ "HSV is possible but less likely, and will show up on biopsy" - but herpes gives painful blisters from the outset rather than a painless depressed spot, and would not track strep throat three times over years. B is the reason a dark vulvar lesion always gets looked at, but melanoma does not recur and resolve, and a 17-year-old is far outside its 50-80 year range. D produces firm, flesh-coloured, dome-shaped umbilicated papules - raised, not depressed, and not post-infectious.

⭐ Treatment is prednisone and vulvar care. Give her 40-60 mg to keep at home and start at the first sign of an outbreak; if they become frequent, consider dapsone.

Principle: a recurrent, post-infectious, initially painless vulvar lesion in a teenager is aphthous - and giving her the steroid to hold at home is the intervention.

stem: You are working as a new resident doctor in the Sexual Assault and Domestic Violence Program at St. Joseph’s hospital. You are assisting in seeing a 26 yr old female patient who was just recently sexually assaulted by an unknown assailant. She is quite distraught, emotional, and frightened. What would be the first step in your assessment of this patient?

options.html: Refer the patient to appropriate mental health professionals and social support groups
Prescribe the morning after pill (levonorgestrel), anti-retroviral medication for HIV prophylaxis, and antibiotics for prophylaxis of chlamydia and gonorrhea.
Perform a detailed history and physical exam, ensuring to gather medically relevant details about the assault and look for corroborating evidence on the physical.

Obtain informed consent from the patient to begin the examination, knowing that the patient may consent to any or all 3 of aspects of the exam: medical exam & tx for the effects of the assault; collection and documentation of medical legal evidence; and disclosure of results to the police for potential legal action.

answer: The correct answer is D. All of these options may be included in your assessment of a sexual assault survivor. However, the most important step is to obtain informed consent from the patient before you begin.

stem: Which of the following are not a characteristic of Progestin?

options.html: Many POCs increase aldosterone production, leading to fluid retention and weight gain.
POCs thicken cervical mucus, making it difficult for sperm penetration
The effect of Progesterone on GnRH suppression is weaker than Estrogen’s effect
When taking POC, patient compliance is not as important

answer: The correct answer is D. It is paramount that POCs are taken at the same time, every single day, because progesterone’s effect on GnRH suppression is “weaker” as it only decreases the chance of ovulation suppression. It heavily relies on its secondary effects (i.e.,thickening of cervical mucus, alteration of tubal peristalsis, suppression of uterine contractility), and therefore these effects wane over time, reverting the endometrium back to the “receptive” condition.

stem: True or False: Taking antibiotics inferes with COCs effectiveness in contraception
answer: The correct answer is B. This is a common myth; there is no clinical relevance between antibiotic consumption & COC’s effectiveness. However, if the patient develops side effect from antibiotics (i.e., vomiting, diarrhea), it may affect plasma concentration of OCPs, therefore making it “less effective”.

stem: Where does capacitation occur?
answer: The correct answer is A. Capacitation is the cellular and molecular changes that ejaculated spermatozoa must undergo in order to fertilize. It occurs while the sperm are in the fallopian tube. It is characterized by three accomplishments: 1) The ability to bind to the zona pellucida (noncellular porous layer of glycoproteins secreted by the oocyte; separates the oocyte from cumulus cells). 2) The ability to undergo acrosomal reaction. 3) The acquisition of hypermotility.

stem: True or false: egg deposited in cul-de-sac by transvaginal injection can never lead to conception.
answer: The correct answer is B. It can in fact be picked up by the fallopian tubes; in fact, some women were shown to achieve pregnancy despite having only one ovary and a single tube located on the contralateral side. The tubal transport is a complex system! It is dependent on 1) ciliary motion, 2) muscular contractility, and 3) tubal fluid →these contribute to varying degrees to effective tubal transport.

stem: Which of the following statements are FALSE?

options.html: Ruptured ovarian cysts are commonly self-limited
Risk of ovarian torsion increases when there is ovarian enlargement
Ectopic pregnancy often leads to ovarian ischemia, resulting in ovarian necrosis, infarction and local hemorrhage
Ovarian torsion can occur in women of all ages

answer: The correct answer is C. Ovarian torsion often results in reduced venous outflow while there is continuous arterial inflow. This leads to ovarian edema →ovarian enlargement →further vascular compression → ovarian ischemia →ovarian necrosis, infarction and local hemorrhage.

stem: First line treatment when endometrial pathology reports atypia endometrial hyperplasia?
answer: The correct answer is A. With atypia, hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is recommended as it is associated with high risk of concurrent or subsequent malignancy. Only when surgery is contraindicated are patients recommended with high dose progesterone treatment. In contrast, typical endometrial hyperplasia is treated with Progesterone (i.e., LN-IUD) & should be followed up usually in 3 months with repeat biopsy.

stem: What is the most common cause of an ectopic pregnancy?
answer: The correct answer is C. Pelvic inflammatory disease is the commonest cause of ectopic pregnancy. Endometriosis and IUD use have also been linked with ectopic pregnancy. Adenomyosis is not a known risk factor for ectopic pregnancy.

stem: Which of the following is true regarding gestational trophoblastic disease?

options.html: The most common site of metastases for choriocarcinoma is the liver
A snowstorm pattern on pelvic ultrasound without a fetus present suggests complete hydatidiform mole
Partial hydatidiform moles contain only paternal chromosomes
After a complete hydatidiform mole, patients should not conceive until at least 3 months after serum beta hCG has returned to baseline

answer:
The correct answer is B.

B is correct. Most common site for choriocarcinoma metastases is the lungs. Partial hydatidiform moles contain 2 sets of paternal chromosomes and 1 set of maternal chromosomes. After a complete hydatidiform mole, patients should abstain from conception for at least a year after serum beta hCG levels have returned to baseline.

stem: In which case would you manage an ectopic pregnancy surgically instead of medically?
answer: The correct answer is B. If the patient’s mass has ruptured, surgical management is indicated. If a patient were hemodynamically unstable, chestfeeding, or non-compliant to follow-up, these would also be indications for surgical management.

stem: A patient presents to your clinic following a D&C with acute pain and urinary retention but no vaginal bleeding. Which complication does she likely have?
answer: The correct answer is B. Patients with hematometra (post-abortal syndrome) commonly present with acute pain and no vaginal bleeding and may have urinary retention as blood accumulates in the uterine cavity. The uterus should be re-evacuated immediately.

stem: Which of the following are the most commonly required supplements in pregnancy
answer: The correct answer is D. Iron and folate are both needed in significant quantities by the developing fetus and are often limited in typical diets worldwide. Calcium, zinc, and vitamin C may be indicated based on maternal issues.

stem: Which of the following vaccinations is recommended in all pregnancies?
answer: The correct answer is A. The pertussis (Tdap) vaccine is recommended at 27-32 weeks to provide passive immunity to the baby as maternal antibodies cross the placenta. MMR and BCC for tuberculosis are contraindicated as they are live attenuated vaccines. Hepatitis A may be indicated in select scenarios but is not recommended for all pregnancies.

answer: The correct answer is C. Once pregnancy has been confirmed, recommended investigations include CBC, Group and Screen, testing for: Rubella, hepatitis B, HIV, VDRL, GC/Chlamydia, and a urine culture. Investigations for gestational diabetes occurs between weeks 24 and 28 of pregnancy.

answer: The correct answer is B. Amenorrhea is common throughout all trimesters. Mood swings and breast tenderness are more commonly experienced in the first trimester. Abdominal bloating is more common in the second and third trimesters.

stem: Which of the following teratogen exposures will pose the greatest risk to the fetus?

options.html: A pregnant patient contracts influenza despite having received the influenza vaccine at 20 weeks gestation
A pregnant patient contracts Rubella at 25 weeks gestation
A pregnant patient starts smoking at 36 weeks gestation
A pregnant patient smokes from conception until they discover they’re pregnant at 10 weeks gestation

answer: The correct answer is D. The purpose of this question is to demonstrate that the greatest sensitivity to teratogens occurs until the 10th week of gestation, as this is when most organogenesis is taking place.

stem: Which of the following is not considered a teratogen?
answer: The correct answer is D. Zika virus is considered the newest addition to “TORCH” infections. Toxoplasmosis is a “TORCH” infection. Hyperthermia can result in spontaneous abortion, neural tube defects, cardiovascular defects, and abdominal wall defects. Acetaminophen is generally considered safe in pregnancy and not a teratogen.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a contraindication to labour?
answer: The correct answer is C. Passage is one of the 4 P’s that influence labour and delivery and refers to the bony pelvis of the mother. Even if the maternal pelvic architecture is not considered favourable for childbirth, this is not a contraindication to labour.

stem: Prior to normal labour, which of the following occurs?

options.html: The cervix becomes thicker and stronger to help push out the baby – this is known as cervical effacement
Braxton-Hicks contractions occur and indicate the onset of labour
The fetal heart rate begins to undergo regular decelerations
The fetal head becomes fixed in the pelvis – this is known as engagement

answer: The correct answer is D. In primiparous women, engagement occurs approximately 2 weeks prior to labour. Cervical effacement describes cervical thinning and softening. Braxton-Hicks contractions do not indicate the onset of labour as they typically begin around the 28th week. The fetal heart rate is monitored during labour and should not undergo regular decelerations in normal labour.

stem: During the 1st stage of labour, which of the following is NOT a consideration?

options.html: More frequent checks of cervical effacement and dilatation improve outcomes
A score of +2 for assessing fetal station indicates the head of the fetus is in the vagina
A fully dilated cervix is approximately 10 cm in diameter
A vaginal exam can assess fetal position, with an anterior occiput being the most favourable for delivery
A fetus with breech presentation may or may not be delivered vaginally

answer: The correct answer is A. More frequent cervical checks increase the likelihood of chorioamnionitis. The remaining answers are true. Some breech presentations can be delivered vaginally, like extended/frank breech, while others are unfavourable, like footling breech.

stem: Which of the following is correct regarding postpartum care?

options.html: Contraception is not required after birth, particularly if a woman is breastfeeding
Per rectum suppositories can help with postpartum hemorrhoids and constipation in 4th degree tears
An initial breastfeed of golden yellow milk is a common sign of mastitis
Sitz baths are recommended for perineal tears

answer: The correct answer is D. Contraception should begin/resume at week 6 postpartum or whenever sexual activity resumes, and lactational amenorrhea from breastfeeding is not fully reliable. Per rectum medications should be avoided in 3rd and 4th degree tears. Golden yellow milk is colostrum, which is produced exclusively in the first several days of breastfeeding postpartum, contains many different immune factors, and is not a sign of mastitis.

stem: Pam, one of your patients, successfully delivered a healthy baby girl, Cece, by spontaneous vaginal delivery 2 days ago. There were no complications and she is ready to be discharged. While her husband Jim searches for their car, she tells you that she already feels drained as she did not sleep well last night. Which of the following statements is NOT true?

options.html: She may experience periods of weepiness and irritability in addition to her insomnia over the next few days, known as the “blues”
She can minimize her sleep disturbances from feedings throughout the night by reducing her exposure to bright lights
Having a baby is a significant life event and is it is normal to experience an adjustment period that may affect her sleep

answer: The correct answer is E. After delivery, Pam will be in a hypoestrogenic state, not hyperestrogenic, that will persist if she is breastfeeding.

stem: Which of the following regarding lactation and milk let-down regulation is true?

options.html: Nipple stimulation inhibits the release of oxytocin
The posterior pituitary releases prolactin to facilitate milk let-down
The anterior pituitary releases oxytocin, which drives lactogenesis
Dopamine levels decrease in response to nipple stimulation and milk removal, which drives an increase in prolactin
Placental delivery drives an increase in progesterone, which facilitates lactogenesis

answer: The correct answer is D. Nipple stimulation increases oxytocin release. The posterior pituitary releases oxytocin to facilitate milk let-down. The anterior pituitary releases prolactin, which drives lactogenesis. Placental delivery causes a decrease in progesterone, which drives an increase in prolactin and lactogenesis.

stem: Rachel has recently become a mother to a healthy baby girl, Emma. Although the pregnancy was unexpected, her partner Ross is ecstatic, despite the 3% chance of pregnancy with their contraceptive of choice. Ross insists that Emma be breastfed, although Rachel is unsure. Which of the follow statements regarding breastfeeding is FALSE and should not be used to help Rachel decide to breastfeed?

options.html: Breastfeeding provides a host of long-term health benefits to both Emma and Rachel
Breastmilk is a sustainable, waste-free, environmentally-friendly practice
Breastmilk is the recommended exclusive nutrition for the first 6 months of life
Breastfeeding is a reliable method of contraception
Colostrum will provide Emma passive immunity to help prevent infections
Breastfeeding can help accelerate Rachel’s recovery from childbirth

answer: The correct answer is D. Breastfeeding can prolong postpartum anovulation and provide some contraceptive benefit but should not be relied on. Contraception should be implemented 6 weeks postpartum or whenever sexual activity resumes.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding normal cardiovascular and pulmonary adaptation is true?

options.html: Surfactant is made in the lungs to increase surface tension within the alveoli
The foramen ovale closes after birth due to increased pulmonary vascular resistance
Lung fluid reabsorption in the neonate is facilitated by ENaC channels within the alveoli
The ductus arteriosus serves to move deoxygenated blood from the right side of the heart to the systemic circulation during fetal development
Normal blood oxygen saturation immediately at birth should be 95+%

answer: The correct answer is C. Surfactant is made in the lungs to decrease surface tension within the alveoli to prevent their collapse. The foramen ovale closes after birth due to decreased pulmonary vascular resistance. The ductus arteriosus serves to move nutrient-rich oxygenated blood from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta during development, allowing the blood to bypass the non-functioning lungs. Normal blood oxygen saturation immediately at birth is 60-65% and normalizes after ~10 minutes.

stem: Which of the following regarding postpartum hemorrhage is FALSE?

options.html: One potential cause of postpartum hemorrhage is retained products
Women with pre-existing coagulopathy, like von Willebrand disease, are at a greater risk of postpartum hemorrhage
Poor lactation is a possible complication of postpartum hemorrhage
Prolonged labour is a protective factor against postpartum hemorrhage as it increases time for hemostasis
Uterine inversion is a serious condition where the uterus turns inside out and is a potential cause of postpartum hemorrhage

answer: The correct answer is D. Prolonged labour can cause uterine muscle exhaustion and is a Tone cause of postpartum hemorrhage. Postpartum hemorrhage causes fall under the 4 T’s: Tone, Tissue, Trauma, and Thrombin. Retained products is a Tissue cause of postpartum hemorrhage. von Willebrand disease is a Thrombin cause of postpartum hemorrhage. Poor lactation following postpartum hemorrhage may represent Sheehan’s syndrome where the pituitary gland infarcts and impacts prolactin-producing cells. Uterine inversion is a Trauma cause of postpartum hemorrhage.

stem: Which of the following is part of the lethal triad of hypovolemic hemorrhagic shock (choose 3):
answer:
The correct answer is A, B, D.

A, B, D are the lethal triad! However, all of the above are indeed signs of hypovolemic shock. Treat the lethal triad by maintaining tissue perfusion (O2, IV fluid, transfusion), warming the patient, and limiting blood loss.

stem: Which of the following should you NOT do for a patient in active hemorrhagic shock?

options.html: Switch patient to a full liquid diet to replenish fluids
Order CBC, lyte, BUN, group and screen, coagulation study, Cr
Call for help and ask for gynecology consult Antepartum hemorrhage:

answer: The correct answer is A. Patient in hypovolemic hemorrhagic shock should be kept NPO instead. Answers B-D should all be done. Ensure to take vitals, maintain ABC, and consult gynecology urgently if the cause is gynecological. Inserting a foley catheter would be important for monitoring urine output.

stem: Which of the following options correctly describes placental abruption, placental previa, placental accreta, or vasa previa (choose 1)?

options.html: Vasa previa involves placental invasion into the myometrium, resulting in a need for hysterectomy
Placental abruption can reliably be diagnosed using the Apt test paired with ultrasound.
Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes will result in the leaking of clear fluid and a positive Kleihaur-Betke test.
The treatment for placental accreta is almost always hysterectomy.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

D is correct. A is incorrect -- it describes placental accreta instead of vasa previa (vasa previa = a condition in which fetal blood vessels cross or run near the internal opening of the uterus). B is incorrect -- placental abruption is actually a diagnosis of exclusion. Ultrasound can be used but we learned in module it isn’t always reliable because the collection of blood may have already drained from the uterus. C is incorrect – preterm prelabour rupture of membranes will indeed result in leakage of clear amniotic fluid. However, Kleihaur-Betke test shows when fetal blood entered maternal circulation! PPROM wouldn’t have a positive Kleihaur-Betke test. D is correct – placental accreta will compromise the uterine myometrium so requires hysterectomy. It doesn’t “always” result in hysterectomy because sometimes invasion is local.

stem: Which statement is FALSE (choose 1)?

options.html: One of the stat investigations to order if there is obstetrical bleed include liver function tests and creatinine.
Cervical dilatation should not be immediately assessed in antepartum hemorrhage
The blood resulting from placental previa is fetal in origin.
Ongoing bleeding can result in reduced clotting abilities (i.e. consumptive disseminated intravascular coagulopathy). Preterm Birth

answer: The correct answer is C. Blood from placental previa is actually maternal in origin. A, B and D are all true. A is true because Creatinine would show kidney function and a liver function test would rule out pre-eclampsia or acute liver injury. B is true because an ultrasound needs to be performed first to confirm the antepartum hemorrhage is not a placental previa (or else assessing for cervical dilation would exacerbate the bleed)

stem: What is the purpose of tocolysis in threatened preterm labour?

options.html: Assist with fetal neuroprotection and prevent possible eclampsia-related seizures (e.g. decreasing risk of cerebral palsy)
Reduce the risk of gram-positive sepsis in neonates

answer: The correct answer is C. Tocolysis slows down active contractions to facilitate transfer to tertiary center and/or administration of antenatal corticosteroids. Answer A is the function of antenatal corticosteroids. C is the function of magnesium sulfate. D is the function of penicillin.

stem: How can preterm birth be prevented?

options.html: All of the above Hypertension in Pregnancy

answer: The correct answer is D. all of the above. Cervicitis (e.g. gonorrhea, chlamydia, bacterial vaginosis, etc.) is a risk factor for preterm birth. Cervical cerclage reduces risk of preterm birth due to cervical insufficiency.

stem: A 40 y.o pregnant mom (in third trimester) presents with headache, blurry vision, fatigue, malaise, nausea/vomiting. She is found to have high liver enzymes, low plt, BP: 130/82. What is her most likely diagnosis, which should not be missed?
answer: The correct answer is A. The patient most likely has HELLP, which stands for hemolysis elevated liver enzymes low plt. Note that it is an typical form of pre-eclampsia/eclampsia so doesn’t require HTN for dx. Molar pregnancy (D) would likely present with extremely high hCG and painless vaginal bleeding. Theca lutein cyst (c) may present with pelvic heaviness, maternal virilization, and ruptured cysts may cause bleeding. Both molar pregnancy and theca lutein cyst would present in earlier pregnancy rather than third trimester and both are risk factors for pre-eclampsia. The patient doesn’t have clinical hypertension/pre-eclampsia though because her BP reading is not over 140/90.

stem: Which of the following is FALSE (choose 1)?

options.html: Comorbid conditions (e.g. diabetes, kidney disease) may increase the risk of severity or progression of pre-eclampsia.
Gestational hypertension can be diagnosed as early as 18 weeks.
Diuretics and ACEi/ARB are contraindicated in hypertensive disorder of pregnancy (HDP).
Severe HDP can result in all of the following: visual disturbances, strokes, cortical blindness, IUGR, oligohydramnios, and hepatic dysfunction. IUGR:

answer: The correct answer is B. Gestational hypertension is diagnosed after 20 weeks (or else it is pre-existing HTN). C is TRUE – diuretics are less effective during pregnancy because pregnancy physiology predisposes to fluid retention. ACEi/ARB are toxic to the fetal kidney. All of the adverse effects of HDP are true in answer D.

stem: Which of the following is the correct order for the progression of placental microvascular damage found on umbilical artery doppler?
answer: The correct answer is B. The first sign of placental microvascular damage is a drop in baseline EDF due to increased resistance to flow. Absent EDF occurs when 50% microvascular structures are damaged. Reversed EDF occurs when 70% of microvasculature is damaged.

stem: Which of the following is FALSE (choose 1)?

options.html: After 20 weeks, the symphysis-fundus height (SFH) correlates to the gestational age (in weeks) so if the SFH is more than 3 cm less than the gestational age, IUGR can be diagnosed.
Very low birth weight is <1500 g and may require intensive care, while extremely low birth weight is <1000 and may require intubation or NG tubes.
Premature babies are defined as small for gestational age (<10%th ile).
If a baby is less than 32 weeks gestational age, delivery is not indicated unless abnormal NST or abnormal UA dopplers.

answer: The correct answer is C. Small for gestational age is not defined by a specific week of gestation. IUGR, SGA and premature are not synonymous terms. A, B and D are correct. D is correct because <32 wks, babies should be monitored in an attempt to remain in utero.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Avalynn is a 40-year-old woman who presents to your office with menorrhagia, cramps and urinary frequency. She is a new patient of yours and has just moved to town. She has had 3 known pregnancy losses in the past without any investigations, and has one child from a teenage pregnancy. On pelvic exam, you find an asymmetrically enlarged bulky uterus. After blood work, you find Alondra to be anemic.

stem: What is the theme of this patient scenario?

options.html: Abnormal uterine bleeding with an enlarged uterus from a structural lesion
Postmenopausal bleeding requiring exclusion of an endometrial malignancy
Chronic pelvic pain with dyspareunia from an inflammatory pelvic process
Secondary amenorrhea with galactorrhea from a hypothalamic-pituitary cause

answer:
The correct answer is A.

She is 40 and still cycling, so this is bleeding within reproductive life rather than after it, and the bimanual finding is the other half of the theme: an asymmetrically enlarged bulky uterus says the cause is structural, sitting in the PALM half of PALM-COEIN rather than the COEIN half.

>

> B is the theme of Case 2, and the contrast between the two is the point of running them together. C describes a different lecture's patient - she has cramps with her menses, not pain between them. D is not bleeding at all.

>

> Principle: name the theme from the bleeding pattern plus the uterus, and the age decides which differential list you reach for.

preamble.html: Avalynn is a 40-year-old woman who presents to your office with menorrhagia, cramps and urinary frequency. She is a new patient of yours and has just moved to town. She has had 3 known pregnancy losses in the past without any investigations, and has one child from a teenage pregnancy. On pelvic exam, you find an asymmetrically enlarged bulky uterus. After blood work, you find Alondra to be anemic.

stem: What are your top 2 differential diagnoses for the theme considering her age?

options.html: Uterine leiomyoma and adenomyosis of the uterus

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Both are structural, both enlarge the uterus, and both bleed heavily - which is exactly why the DSSG asks for two rather than one.

>

> ⭐ The uterine contour separates them. Fibroids produce an irregular / asymmetric uterus; adenomyosis produces a globally enlarged, boggy one. Avalynn's is asymmetric, so leiomyoma leads.

>

> The rest of her story points the same way: pressure symptoms (urinary frequency) and recurrent pregnancy loss. ⭐ Of the four structural lesions in 13 - Approach to Pathology of AUB & Pelvic Pain, endometriosis, polyps and leiomyomas cause infertility - adenomyosis does NOT. Her three losses therefore favour the fibroid twice over.

>

> A is Case 2's list and needs a postmenopausal patient. C and D do not give an asymmetric bulky uterus.

>

> Principle: asymmetric uterus plus pregnancy loss is leiomyoma; globally boggy without infertility is adenomyosis.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Avalynn is a 40-year-old woman who presents to your office with menorrhagia, cramps and urinary frequency. She is a new patient of yours and has just moved to town. She has had 3 known pregnancy losses in the past without any investigations, and has one child from a teenage pregnancy. On pelvic exam, you find an asymmetrically enlarged bulky uterus. After blood work, you find Alondra to be anemic.

stem: What is your approach and investigative plan (i.e. diagnostic pathway) for Avalynn?

options.html: Transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial biopsy without any preceding bloodwork
CA-125, CT of the chest abdomen and pelvis, then gynecologic oncology referral
Pregnancy test, CBC, pelvic exam and pelvic ultrasound as first-line imaging
Hysteroscopy with dilation and curettage as the initial diagnostic procedure

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The order matters more than the list. ⭐ A pregnancy test comes first in any reproductive-age woman who is bleeding - she is 40 and has conceived before. The CBC is already abnormal, which is what makes her anemia part of the workup rather than an incidental finding, and pelvic ultrasound is the first-line imaging for a structurally enlarged uterus.

>

> Hysteroscopy or endometrial biopsy is the second step, not the first - considered if there is concern for intrauterine pathology once the ultrasound has been seen. That is what makes D premature.

>

> A skips the pregnancy test. B is Case 3's pathway and treats a benign structural picture as an ovarian malignancy.

>

> Principle: pregnancy test, bloods, examination, ultrasound - then decide whether the endometrium needs sampling.

She has had 3 known pregnancy losses in the past without any investigations, and has one child from a teenage pregnancy. On pelvic exam, you find an asymmetrically enlarged bulky uterus. After blood work, you find Alondra to be anemic.

stem: Name the three locations in the uterus for this entity.
answer:
The correct answer is D.

The three locations are named for the layer the fibroid sits against, and ⭐ each location predicts a different symptom:

>

> | Location | Where | What it does |

> | --- | --- | --- |

> | Submucosal | beneath the endometrium | ⭐ most associated with bleeding and infertility |

> | Intramural | within the myometrium | ⭐ the most common |

> | Subserosal | beneath the serosal surface | ⭐ more pressure symptoms |

>

> Avalynn has both halves: heavy bleeding with pregnancy loss (submucosal) and urinary frequency (subserosal), which is why a single uterus can carry more than one fibroid and more than one symptom.

>

> Principle: the layer names the symptom - submucosal bleeds, subserosal presses, intramural is simply commonest.

She has had 3 known pregnancy losses in the past without any investigations, and has one child from a teenage pregnancy. On pelvic exam, you find an asymmetrically enlarged bulky uterus. After blood work, you find Alondra to be anemic.

stem: Why do these lesions cause bleeding?

options.html: They increase endometrial surface area and distort the cavity
They erode the cervical epithelium and produce contact bleeding
They raise circulating estrogen and drive endometrial proliferation
They consume platelets locally and create a consumptive coagulopathy

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Four mechanisms, and they are structural rather than hormonal:

>

> - Increase endometrial surface area - more lining to shed

> - Distort the uterine cavity

> - Interfere with normal uterine contraction - the myometrium cannot clamp down on the vessels

> - Cause abnormal vasculature

>

> Together: heavy, prolonged menstrual bleeding.

>

> C is the trap worth naming - fibroids are estrogen-responsive, which is why they regress after menopause and why GnRH analogues shrink them, but they do not cause a systemic estrogen excess. The bleeding is mechanical. B describes a cervical lesion. D is a coagulopathy, the C of PALM-COEIN.

>

> Principle: fibroids bleed for mechanical reasons - more surface, a distorted cavity, a myometrium that cannot contract.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Karen is a 60 year old woman who presents to your family practice office with vaginal bleeding that has lasted over a week. Her last menstrual period was 8 years ago, so she finds this unexpected bleeding distressing. Karen has been your patient for many years and her only health problem has been a high body mass index (BMI). She has an infertility history and has one daughter conceived by in vitro fertilization. She has a family history of colon cancer in a brother at age 58 and endometrial cancer in a sister at age 55. You find the speculum examination to be normal with no active bleeding. Bi-manual examination reveals a slightly enlarged uterus.

stem: What is the theme of this patient scenario?

options.html: Abnormal uterine bleeding from a structural lesion before menopause
Postmenopausal bleeding in a woman carrying several risk factors
Perimenopausal anovulatory bleeding as her ovarian reserve declines
Atrophic vaginitis producing postcoital spotting after the menopause

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Her last menstrual period was 8 years ago, so any bleeding now is by definition postmenopausal.

>

> ⭐ Any postmenopausal bleeding should be treated as endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. That sentence is the whole theme - it is not a differential, it is a rule about where the workup starts.

>

> A is Case 1. C would require her still to be cycling. D is on the differential list but is not the theme, and settling on it early is precisely the error the rule exists to prevent.

>

> Principle: bleeding after 12 months of amenorrhea is cancer until the endometrium says otherwise.

stem: What is your differential diagnosis for the theme considering her age? Contrast your list with case 1.

options.html: Leiomyoma, adenomyosis, endometrial polyp and chronic endometritis
Ectopic pregnancy, threatened abortion and retained products of conception
Endometrial carcinoma, hyperplasia, polyp, atrophy and cervical cancer
Ovarian carcinoma, tubo-ovarian abscess and a pedunculated fibroid

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The list and the contrast are one answer. Karen's differential is endometrial carcinoma, endometrial hyperplasia, endometrial polyp, endometrial atrophy, cervical cancer and hormone therapy effects.

>

> | | Case 1 - Avalynn | Case 2 - Karen |

> | --- | --- | --- |

> | Menopausal status | Premenopausal | Postmenopausal |

> | Commonest cause | Fibroids | ⭐ Endometrial cancer is the concern |

> | Weight of concern | Benign structural disease | ⭐ Malignancy |

>

> ⚠ Atrophy is worth keeping on the list even though cancer drives the workup - it is a common benign cause of postmenopausal bleeding, and finding it is a diagnosis rather than a failure to find cancer.

>

> A is Case 1's list. B needs a pregnant patient. D presents as a mass, not as bleeding.

>

> Principle: the same symptom changes differential entirely across the menopause - that is why the DSSG asks you to contrast.

Bi-manual examination reveals a slightly enlarged uterus.

stem: What is your approach and investigative plan (i.e. diagnostic pathway) for Karen?

options.html: Pregnancy test, CBC and pelvic ultrasound, with sampling only if imaging is abnormal
CA-125 with CT of the chest abdomen and pelvis, then gynecologic oncology referral
Reassurance and review in three months, since her speculum examination was normal
Pelvic exam, transvaginal ultrasound for endometrial thickness, endometrial biopsy

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Three steps, and the third is not conditional on the second.

>

> 1. Pelvic examination

> 2. Transvaginal ultrasound, to measure the endometrial thickness

> 3. Endometrial biopsy

>

> ⚠ B is the trap, and it is a subtle one. Measuring the stripe and sampling only if it is thick is a reasonable algorithm in some settings, but Karen carries a family history suggestive of Lynch syndrome on top of obesity and infertility, and a pregnancy test at 60 with an LMP 8 years ago is not a step. The tissue is what settles it.

>

> B stages a cancer that has not been diagnosed. C is the one answer that is unsafe - ⚠ a normal speculum examination excludes a cervical or vaginal source, not an endometrial one.

>

> Principle: in postmenopausal bleeding the ultrasound guides, and the biopsy decides.

preamble.html: Karen is a 60 year old woman who presents to your family practice office with vaginal bleeding that has lasted over a week. Her last menstrual period was 8 years ago, so she finds this unexpected bleeding distressing. Karen has been your patient for many years and her only health problem has been a high body mass index (BMI). She has an infertility history and has one daughter conceived by in vitro fertilization. She has a family history of colon cancer in a brother at age 58 and endometrial cancer in a sister at age 55. You find the speculum examination to be normal with no active bleeding. Bi-manual examination reveals a slightly enlarged uterus.

stem: The ultrasound shows 10 mm endometrial lining thickness. The results come back from pathology and the report reads unsatisfactory for diagnosis due to insufficient tissue. What should you consider given this information and what is your next step?

options.html: The stripe is abnormal and an insufficient sample cannot exclude cancer
The stripe is normal for her age, so the insufficient sample can safely be observed
The insufficient sample indicates an atrophic endometrium, which explains the bleeding
The stripe is abnormal but a repeat biopsy adds nothing, so proceed to hysterectomy

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Two facts have to be held at once, and the DSSG asks for both.

>

> ⭐ A postmenopausal woman should normally have an endometrial stripe of about ≤4 mm. 10 mm is abnormal.

>

> ⭐ An "insufficient sample" does not rule out cancer. It is a failed test, not a negative one - and pairing a failed test with an abnormal ultrasound is what makes standing still unacceptable.

>

> The next step is therefore either repeat sampling or hysteroscopy with dilation and curettage (D&C), which has the advantage of seeing the cavity while sampling it.

>

> B misreads the cutoff. C turns a failed test into a diagnosis. D skips to definitive surgery without tissue.

>

> Principle: a non-diagnostic sample against an abnormal stripe means sample again - it never means reassure.

She has a family history of colon cancer in a brother at age 58 and endometrial cancer in a sister at age 55. You find the speculum examination to be normal with no active bleeding. Bi-manual examination reveals a slightly enlarged uterus.

stem: The results come back from pathology and the report reads "atypical endometrial hyperplasia". What is your next step and why?

options.html: A levonorgestrel intrauterine system, with repeat sampling in three to six months
Total hysterectomy, usually with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy after menopause
High dose oral megestrol, reserving surgery for failure of medical management
Repeat the endometrial biopsy in six months to confirm the atypia is persistent

answer:
The correct answer is B.

⭐ Modern terminology for this is endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia (EIN), and the reason it is managed surgically is not the risk of *becoming* cancer - it is the chance that it already is.

>

> - High risk of progression to carcinoma

> - ⭐ A significant proportion already have occult carcinoma at the time of diagnosis, which sampling has missed

>

> So the next step is total hysterectomy, and in a postmenopausal woman usually with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

>

> ⭐ B and C are the right answers to a different question. Hyperplasia without atypia, or a woman who wants to preserve fertility, is managed medically - and there the levonorgestrel IUS is first line. Karen is 60 with atypia, so neither applies. D watches a lesion that may already be carcinoma.

>

> Principle: atypia sends the uterus to the operating room because the biopsy may have undercalled a cancer.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Karen is a 60 year old woman who presents to your family practice office with vaginal bleeding that has lasted over a week. Her last menstrual period was 8 years ago, so she finds this unexpected bleeding distressing. Karen has been your patient for many years and her only health problem has been a high body mass index (BMI). She has an infertility history and has one daughter conceived by in vitro fertilization. She has a family history of colon cancer in a brother at age 58 and endometrial cancer in a sister at age 55. You find the speculum examination to be normal with no active bleeding. Bi-manual examination reveals a slightly enlarged uterus.

stem: What will you plan to discuss (as her specialist) with Karen regarding her further management and outlook?

options.html: Primary chemoradiation, with surgery reserved for residual disease after treatment
Cytoreductive surgery followed by carboplatin and paclitaxel, with a poor prognosis
Surgical staging with hysterectomy and BSO, nodal assessment, and a good prognosis
Hormonal therapy alone, given that her disease was detected at an early stage

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The management conversation and the prognosis conversation are different halves of the same answer.

>

> Management - total hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, lymph node assessment, then radiation, chemotherapy or hormonal therapy depending on what the staging shows.

>

> Outlook - ⭐ often good, because postmenopausal bleeding causes early presentation. That is the sentence worth carrying: the symptom is alarming, and being alarming is what makes the cancer curable.

>

> B is Case 3's answer, and the contrast is deliberate - ⭐ endometrial cancer announces itself and ovarian cancer does not, which is why one presents early and the other at stage III. A and D are not primary management here.

>

> Principle: endometrial cancer is surgically staged, and its prognosis is good for the same reason it was found.

preamble.html: Karen is a 60 year old woman who presents to your family practice office with vaginal bleeding that has lasted over a week. Her last menstrual period was 8 years ago, so she finds this unexpected bleeding distressing. Karen has been your patient for many years and her only health problem has been a high body mass index (BMI). She has an infertility history and has one daughter conceived by in vitro fertilization. She has a family history of colon cancer in a brother at age 58 and endometrial cancer in a sister at age 55. You find the speculum examination to be normal with no active bleeding. Bi-manual examination reveals a slightly enlarged uterus.

stem: What are risk factors for the development of Karen's cancer?

options.html: Multiparity, early menopause and long term combined oral contraceptive use
Smoking, high grade HPV infection and immunosuppression after transplantation
BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations, nulliparity and a long uninterrupted ovulatory life
Excess estrogen unopposed by progesterone, plus Lynch syndrome in her family

answer:
The correct answer is D.

⭐ One idea generates most of the list: estrogen without progesterone.

>

> Obesity · nulliparity · infertility · late menopause · estrogen therapy · tamoxifen

>

> Karen carries obesity and infertility from that list outright.

>

> Then the family history, which is the second half of the answer. A brother with colon cancer at 58 and a sister with endometrial cancer at 55 is the pattern of ⭐ Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) - two Lynch-spectrum cancers in first-degree relatives, both young. That is a genetics referral, and it changes surveillance for her whole family, not just her treatment.

>

> C is the ovarian list. B is cervical. A inverts every item - those are protective.

>

> Principle: unopposed estrogen explains the sporadic case; two young Lynch-spectrum cancers explain the familial one.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Adella, a 55 year old woman, presents to you, her family doctor, with abdominal discomfort and increasing girth which have been getting worse over the last few weeks. She also complains of urinary frequency, constipation and early satiety, which she assumed was due to aging. Adella's last menstrual period was 8 months ago and she has no children. On physical exam, bilateral adnexal masses are palpated.

stem: What are the clues on history and physical exam which help formulate your differential diagnosis?

options.html: Perimenopausal age, nulliparity, bilateral masses, progressive symptoms
Reproductive age, high parity, a unilateral mass and acute onset of the pain
Cyclical pain, dyspareunia and a fixed retroverted uterus on bimanual exam
Postmenopausal bleeding, obesity and a family history of endometrial cancer

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Adella's clues are worth listing because ⭐ every one of them is vague on its own and specific together:

>

> - Postmenopausal / perimenopausal age - her LMP was 8 months ago

> - ⭐ Bilateral masses - bilaterality is the finding that pushes hardest toward malignancy

> - Abdominal distension and increasing girth

> - Ascites symptoms - early satiety, constipation, urinary frequency

> - Progressive symptoms over weeks

> - Nulliparity

>

> ⚠ She assumed it was aging, and that is the clinical lesson rather than an aside. Ovarian cancer presents through symptoms every older person has, which is why it reaches stage III before anyone names it.

>

> D is Karen. B and C describe patients from other Week 4 lectures.

>

> Principle: bloating, early satiety and urinary frequency that are new and progressive in an older woman are an ovarian history until imaged.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Adella, a 55 year old woman, presents to you, her family doctor, with abdominal discomfort and increasing girth which have been getting worse over the last few weeks. She also complains of urinary frequency, constipation and early satiety, which she assumed was due to aging. Adella's last menstrual period was 8 months ago and she has no children. On physical exam, bilateral adnexal masses are palpated.

stem: What is your differential diagnosis for Adella's pelvic masses?

options.html: Leiomyoma, adenomyosis and a pedunculated subserosal fibroid undergoing torsion
Benign epithelial tumours, endometrioma, the ovarian carcinomas, and metastases
Tubo-ovarian abscess, hydrosalpinx and pelvic inflammatory disease with adhesions
Functional ovarian cysts, corpus luteum cyst and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

answer:
The correct answer is B.

The list runs benign to malignant to metastatic, and at 55 with bilateral masses the weight sits at the malignant end:

>

> | Benign | Malignant | Other |

> | --- | --- | --- |

> | Serous cystadenoma | High-grade serous carcinoma | Metastatic disease |

> | Mucinous cystadenoma | Endometrioid carcinoma | |

> | Endometrioma | Mucinous carcinoma | |

>

> ⚠ Metastatic disease belongs on the list and is the one most often dropped. Bilateral ovarian masses are a classic site for secondary spread, and a gastric primary is the named example.

>

> D would be the list in a much younger woman. A is uterine rather than adnexal. C is an infective picture with pain and fever, not painless progressive distension.

>

> Principle: an adnexal mass differential is read off age - functional in the young, neoplastic in the old.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Adella, a 55 year old woman, presents to you, her family doctor, with abdominal discomfort and increasing girth which have been getting worse over the last few weeks. She also complains of urinary frequency, constipation and early satiety, which she assumed was due to aging. Adella's last menstrual period was 8 months ago and she has no children. On physical exam, bilateral adnexal masses are palpated.

stem: What is your approach and investigative plan (i.e. diagnostic pathway) for Adella?

options.html: Pelvic ultrasound and endometrial biopsy, with a hysteroscopy if the sample fails
Laparoscopy with ovarian cystectomy to obtain tissue before any imaging is ordered
Pelvic ultrasound, CA-125, CT of chest abdomen and pelvis, and oncology referral
Serial ultrasound at three and six months to see whether the masses are enlarging

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Pelvic ultrasound · CA-125 · CT chest / abdomen / pelvis · gynecologic oncology referral.

>

> ⭐ The referral is part of the pathway, not something that follows it. Suspected ovarian malignancy goes to gynae oncology before surgery, because the operation that stages and debulks is a different operation from the one a general gynecologist would do - and doing the wrong one first worsens the outcome.

>

> ⚠ B is Karen's pathway applied to the wrong organ. B is the specific trap: ⭐ cutting into a possible ovarian malignancy to get tissue risks spilling it, and staging depends on whether the capsule was intact. D watches a probable cancer.

>

> ⚠ The vault's own ovarian cancer note is thin on this pathway - it carries CA-125 as a tumour marker but not the sequence - so the order above is the DSSG's, and worth confirming with the facilitator.

>

> Principle: image it, mark it, stage it, and refer before anyone operates.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Adella is back in your office two weeks later to discuss her test results. Serum CA-125 is elevated. Ultrasound shows solid bilateral 8 cm complex cystic and solid tubo-ovarian masses. CT scan shows omental changes of possible metastases and ascites.

stem: What are your next steps for Adella?

options.html: Neoadjuvant carboplatin and paclitaxel, with surgery only if she responds
Image guided biopsy of an omental nodule, then wait for the full pathology
Paracentesis for symptom relief, with cytology to establish the diagnosis
Exploratory surgery with surgical staging and cytoreduction, or debulking

answer:
The correct answer is D.

The findings have converted suspicion into a working diagnosis: ⭐ an elevated CA-125, bilateral complex masses, omental disease and ascites are highly suspicious for advanced ovarian carcinoma.

>

> The next step is exploratory surgery, which does three jobs at once:

>

> - Diagnosis - tissue

> - Surgical staging

> - ⭐ Cytoreduction (debulking) - and in ovarian cancer the volume of residual disease left behind is itself prognostic, which is why the operation is therapeutic and not merely diagnostic

>

> A is a real pathway for patients who cannot be optimally debulked up front, but the DSSG's answer here is primary surgery. B and C obtain tissue without treating anything.

>

> Principle: in advanced ovarian cancer the staging operation is also the first line of treatment.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: At surgery, there are bilateral tubo-ovarian masses with surface involvement, omental nodules and 1 L of ascites.

stem: What is the most likely diagnosis based on the findings?

options.html: High-grade serous carcinoma of the ovary
Metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma to both ovaries
Bilateral mucinous cystadenoma of the ovaries
Endometrioid carcinoma arising in an endometrioma

answer:
The correct answer is A.

⭐ High-grade serous carcinoma is the most common ovarian cancer, and every operative finding fits it:

>

> - Bilateral masses

> - Surface involvement

> - Ascites

> - Omental metastases

>

> B is the one that must stay in mind - bilateral ovarian masses are a classic metastatic site - but nothing in her story points at a gastric primary, and the surface and omental pattern is primary peritoneal spread. C is benign and would not produce omental nodules. D usually arises on a background of endometriosis, which she does not have.

>

> Principle: bilateral, surface-involving, omental and ascitic is high-grade serous until the pathology says otherwise.

lectureMeta: Q23-Q46, stems verbatim from `p2_repro_dssg_-_student_2026.docx` (Drs. J. Walsh, M. Weir), read from OneNote B2 Repro / Synch W4. Keyed from the session's worked answers.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: At surgery, there are bilateral tubo-ovarian masses with surface involvement, omental nodules and 1 L of ascites.

stem: What will you (as the oncologist) plan to discuss with Adella regarding her management, outlook and risk factors?

options.html: Hysterectomy with nodal assessment, a good outlook, and unopposed estrogen risks
Debulking and carboplatin-paclitaxel, a guarded outlook, risk factors
Radiation with concurrent cisplatin, an excellent outlook, and HPV vaccination
Hormonal therapy and surveillance, an excellent outlook, and smoking cessation

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Three conversations:

>

> Management - cytoreductive surgery, carboplatin + paclitaxel, and ⭐ PARP inhibitors if she carries a BRCA mutation, which is why the genetic result is a treatment decision and not only a family one.

>

> Outlook - guarded. ⭐ Many ovarian cancers are diagnosed at stage III because the symptoms are vague, and hers were dismissed as aging.

>

> Risk factors - increasing age · nulliparity · infertility · BRCA1 · BRCA2 · family history. ⭐ And the protective ones are worth saying out loud, because they share a mechanism: OCP use, pregnancy and breastfeeding all suppress ovulation.

>

> A is Karen's. C is cervical. D treats an advanced carcinoma with surveillance.

>

> Principle: fewer lifetime ovulations means lower risk - which is why nulliparity raises it and the pill lowers it.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: You are a consulting physician on your weekly rounds in the local nursing home. One of your patients, Bea, is an 82 year old bed-ridden retired nurse. One of her caregivers has identified a mass in her left groin when bathing her and she has brought this to your attention. Upon physical exam, you detect a 4 cm firm, painless mass in Bea's left groin, which is situated deeply, and the overlying skin appears normal.

stem: What is your differential diagnosis for the groin mass considering her age?

options.html: Femoral artery aneurysm, saphena varix and a psoas abscess tracking down
Incarcerated femoral hernia, hydrocele of the canal of Nuck and a seroma
Metastatic cancer, lymphoma, reactive lymphadenopathy, hernia and lipoma
Reactive lymphadenopathy from cellulitis, an abscess and an infected cyst

answer:
The correct answer is C.

At 82 the list is led by malignancy, but it stays broad:

>

> Metastatic cancer · lymphoma · reactive lymphadenopathy · hernia · lipoma

>

> ⭐ Her described features already narrow it before any test. A mass that is firm, painless, deeply situated and covered by normal skin is behaving like a node rather than like an infection or a hernia - and a painless firm node in an 82-year-old is malignant until proven otherwise.

>

> A and B are vascular and hernia-weighted lists that leave malignancy out. D is the infective list, and reactive nodes are usually tender with a source to find.

>

> Principle: firm, painless and fixed in an older patient means node, and node means find the primary.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: You are a consulting physician on your weekly rounds in the local nursing home. One of your patients, Bea, is an 82 year old bed-ridden retired nurse. One of her caregivers has identified a mass in her left groin when bathing her and she has brought this to your attention. Upon physical exam, you detect a 4 cm firm, painless mass in Bea's left groin, which is situated deeply, and the overlying skin appears normal.

stem: What is your initial approach to Bea?

options.html: Urgent excisional biopsy of the groin mass to obtain a tissue diagnosis first
A CT of the abdomen and pelvis to look for an intra-abdominal primary tumour
A trial of oral antibiotics with review in two weeks if the mass has not settled
A full history and complete examination, including the skin the node drains

answer:
The correct answer is D.

⭐ The initial approach to a lymph node is to examine the territory it drains. The inguinal nodes drain the vulva, the lower vagina, the perianal region, the anal canal and the lower limb - so the examination that matters is of skin and mucosa, not of the node itself.

>

> ⚠ Bea is bed-ridden in a nursing home, which is the reason this matters. A vulvar lesion on a bed-bound 82-year-old can go unlooked-at for a long time, and the caregiver found the node before anyone found the primary.

>

> A inverts the order - characterise before you excise, and ⭐ FNA comes before excisional biopsy for a node suspected of carrying metastatic carcinoma. B searches the wrong compartment first. C treats a painless firm node as an infection.

>

> Principle: when you find the node, examine what drains into it before you image or cut.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: You are a consulting physician on your weekly rounds in the local nursing home. One of your patients, Bea, is an 82 year old bed-ridden retired nurse. One of her caregivers has identified a mass in her left groin when bathing her and she has brought this to your attention. Upon physical exam, you detect a 4 cm firm, painless mass in Bea's left groin, which is situated deeply, and the overlying skin appears normal.

stem: Given that the mass is firm, non-cystic, non-pulsating without bruits or bowel sounds what is your investigative plan (i.e. diagnostic pathway) for Bea?

options.html: Fine needle aspiration of the node, with imaging once cytology is back
Ultrasound of the groin followed by observation if it appears to be a lipoma
Incision and drainage of the mass, sending any fluid obtained for culture
Whole body PET-CT as the first investigation to locate an occult primary

answer:
The correct answer is A.

⭐ The wording of the stem is the reasoning, not scene-setting. Each negative removes something:

>

> | Finding | What it rules out |

> | --- | --- |

> | Non-cystic | an abscess or a cyst |

> | Non-pulsating, no bruits | a femoral artery aneurysm |

> | No bowel sounds | a hernia containing bowel |

> | Firm | leaves a solid mass, most likely a node |

>

> What remains is a solid node, and the next move is fine needle aspiration for a cytological diagnosis - it is quick, it is tolerable in a frail bed-bound patient, and ⭐ knowing the cell type redirects the entire search.

>

> C would be right for the abscess the examination has already excluded.

>

> Principle: the physical examination is a series of exclusions, and FNA answers what is left.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: You are a consulting physician on your weekly rounds in the local nursing home. One of your patients, Bea, is an 82 year old bed-ridden retired nurse. One of her caregivers has identified a mass in her left groin when bathing her and she has brought this to your attention. Upon physical exam, you detect a 4 cm firm, painless mass in Bea's left groin, which is situated deeply, and the overlying skin appears normal.

stem: You perform a fine needle aspiration biopsy. The pathologist reports the cytological diagnosis as "squamous cell carcinoma". What is the most likely site of origin?

options.html: The endometrium, cervix or fallopian tube on the ipsilateral left side
The vulva, lower vagina, perianal region, anal canal or lower limb
The stomach, pancreas or colon, spreading through the abdominal nodes
The lung or breast, which metastasise widely to the nodal basins first

answer:
The correct answer is B.

⭐ The cell type plus the node's drainage territory gives the answer. Squamous cell carcinoma arises from squamous epithelium, so the primary must be somewhere squamous that drains to the inguinal nodes:

>

> Vulva · lower vagina · perianal region · anal canal · lower extremities

>

> ⭐ In gynecology, vulvar squamous cell carcinoma is the classic answer.

>

> ⚠ Note where the boundary falls. The lower vagina drains to the inguinal nodes; the upper vagina, cervix and uterus drain to the pelvic nodes. That anatomical split is what makes A wrong rather than merely unlikely.

>

> C would give adenocarcinoma, not squamous. D is a distant-metastasis list that skips the drainage logic.

>

> Principle: squamous cytology in an inguinal node points below the pelvic floor, not above it.

The correct answer is C.

⭐ Primary vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, and the vault's own lecture explains why she is the patient for it.

> 14 - Vulvar Lesions and Vulvar Cancer splits vulvar SCC into two opposite types, and ⭐ the non-HPV type is the one that fits Bea: older women, a SOLITARY lesion, on the vestibule and labia minora, often on a background of lichen sclerosus or lichen planus, and ⭐ biopsy often shows INVASION already. The note's own line is that the non-HPV, older, solitary, lichen-associated lesion is the dangerous one.

>

> Two further points from that note explain how it got this far: ⭐ 50% of women with vulvar cancer are asymptomatic, and where there are symptoms pruritus is the commonest complaint - the same symptom as every benign vulvar condition.
