Upon physical exam, you detect a 4 cm firm, painless mass in Bea's left groin, which is situated deeply, and the overlying skin appears normal.

stem: What is/are your next step(s)?

options.html: Immediate radical vulvectomy with bilateral inguinofemoral node dissection
Primary chemoradiation without biopsy, given the FNA already shows carcinoma
Palliative care alone, given her age and her bed-bound functional status
Complete vulvar examination, biopsy, staging imaging and oncology referral

The correct answer is D.

In order: complete vulvar examination · biopsy of the vulvar lesion · imaging for staging · gynecologic oncology referral - and then surgical excision ± lymph node dissection, with radiation or chemotherapy depending on stage.

>

> ⭐ The FNA diagnosed the node, not the primary. The vulvar lesion still needs its own biopsy, because the primary's histology and margins drive the operation.

>

> A operates before staging. B skips the tissue that plans the treatment.

>

> ⚠ D deserves a straight answer rather than dismissal. Bea is 82, bed-bound and frail, so ⭐ her fitness genuinely shapes what is offered - a less radical operation, or radiation instead of surgery. But that is a decision made after staging and with her, not a reason to skip the diagnosis. Withholding a workup on age alone is the error this option is here to name.

>

> Principle: frailty changes which treatment is right, not whether the cancer gets diagnosed and staged.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Caroline, an 18-year-old college student, presents to the student health office for counselling on contraceptives methods. She has not yet been sexually active but is currently in a healthy three-month relationship and wishes to take extra precaution in case they decide to become intimate. Her past medical history is unremarkable, and she does not smoke. Her menses have always been quite regular, with cycles ranging between 28 and 30 days. She has never had a pap test and has bever been diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection. She asks you about the difference between Yasmin® and Micronor®.

stem: Explain to Carolina the differences between Yasmin® and Micronor® in terms of their mechanism of action and common adverse effects.

options.html: Yasmin suppresses ovulation centrally; Micronor acts mainly locally
Both suppress ovulation centrally, differing only in their estrogen content
Yasmin acts on cervical mucus; Micronor suppresses ovulation centrally
Both act only locally, but Yasmin adds an anti-mineralocorticoid effect

answer:
The correct answer is A.

This is the one CBL question the deck answers outright, and the mechanisms are genuinely different in kind, not degree.

>

> | | Yasmin | Micronor |

> | --- | --- | --- |

> | Contents | ethinyl estradiol 30 mcg + drospirenone 3 mg | norethindrone 0.35 mg |

> | Mechanism | ⭐ primarily CENTRAL - suppresses GnRH, so LH and FSH fall and ovulation stops | ⭐ primarily LOCAL - thickened cervical mucus, thinned endometrium, reduced tubal cilia activity |

> | Ovulation | consistently suppressed | ⭐ suppressed in only about 50% of cycles |

>

> ⭐ That the progestin-only mechanism is local rather than central is the single most-tested fact in this lecture, and it is what makes timing matter so much more for the mini-pill: ⚠ missed by more than 3 hours means backup contraception.

>

> Adverse effects. Yasmin carries the estrogen profile - ⭐ increased venous thromboembolism risk (estrogen raises factors VII, VIII, IX and X and lowers the anticoagulant factors), nausea, bloating, breast tenderness, headache, and hepatic metabolism giving cytochrome P450 interactions. ⭐ Drospirenone is the anti-androgenic progestin, derived from spironolactone - which is why it helps acne and why it risks hyperkalemia. Micronor carries no increased VTE risk and irregular bleeding instead.

>

> The deck's own closing point on Caroline: no contraindication to either type, and a similar failure rate.

>

> Principle: combined is central and estrogen-carrying; progestin-only is local and forgiving of everything except the clock.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Caroline is now in her last year of the Nursing program. She tells you that with her night shifts in the hospital, she has been forgetting to take her contraceptive pills (Yasmin). She had unprotected intercourse 3 days ago and can’t remember when was the last day she took her pill. She asks you about emergency contraceptive options and other options for contraceptive methods. Her medical history is unremarkable. However, she gained significant weight in the past few years.

stem: How do emergency contraceptive methods work to prevent pregnancy? Compare Levonorgestrel and Ulipristal acetate in terms of their mechanism, timing, and efficacy.

options.html: Both terminate an established pregnancy, and ulipristal is the more effective
Both suppress the LH surge; ulipristal also blocks rupture and lasts 120 hours
Both prevent implantation; levonorgestrel lasts 120 hours and ulipristal 72
Both block fertilisation directly, with identical windows and identical efficacy

answer:
The correct answer is B.

⭐ Emergency contraception works by delaying or preventing ovulation, not by disturbing an implanted pregnancy. ⚠ No emergency contraceptive works once implantation has happened - only mifepristone acts on an established pregnancy, which is what makes A wrong in principle rather than in detail.

>

> | | Levonorgestrel | Ulipristal acetate |

> | --- | --- | --- |

> | Window | ≤ 72 h | ⭐ ≤ 120 h (5 days) |

> | Class | progesterone receptor agonist | selective progesterone receptor modulator |

> | Mechanism | suppress the LH surge | suppress the LH surge plus a direct ovarian action preventing follicle rupture |

> | Pregnancy rate 0-24 h | 2.5% | 0.9% (odds ratio 0.35, *p* = 0.035) |

>

> The timing follows from the biology the deck puts up first: an egg lives 12-24 hours after ovulation, sperm live about 5 days, so the fertile window is about 6 days. Buying time against ovulation is the whole mechanism.

>

> ⚠ ⭐ Ulipristal beats levonorgestrel at every interval, including inside 72 hours - an Elentra module question keys this the other way, and the lecture's own meta-analysis slide is the one to trust.

>

> Principle: both delay ovulation; ulipristal has the longer window, the extra ovarian action and the better numbers.

Her medical history is unremarkable. However, she gained significant weight in the past few years.

stem: Given Caroline's situation, which of these emergency contraception options would potentially still be effective?

options.html: Levonorgestrel alone, since 72 hours has not yet elapsed
Levonorgestrel and ulipristal, both still inside their windows
Ulipristal acetate, and a copper intrauterine device
Neither, because her fertile window has already closed

answer:
The correct answer is C.

3 days is 72 hours, which is exactly the edge of the levonorgestrel window and comfortably inside ulipristal's.

>

> - Ulipristal - ⭐ licensed to 120 hours, so she has two days in hand

> - Copper IUD - ⭐ the most effective of the three, non-hormonal, working through an inflammatory uterine environment with copper toxic to sperm and blastocyst. It also becomes her ongoing contraception, which matters for someone whose problem is remembering a daily pill

>

> A relies on being at the very limit of the window, and B treats that limit as comfortable. ⚠ The deck itself only lists LNG and UPA on this slide - ⭐ the copper IUD is on the lecture note's emergency contraception table and is the most effective option, so leaving it off the answer would lose the best one.

>

> ⚠ Her weight is not what settles this. The vault's note records reduced efficacy at higher weight for the patch, not for emergency contraception, so the timing is the argument here. Worth raising with the facilitator.

>

> Principle: at 72 hours reach past levonorgestrel - ulipristal has the window and the copper IUD has both the efficacy and the future.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Caroline is now in her last year of the Nursing program. She tells you that with her night shifts in the hospital, she has been forgetting to take her contraceptive pills (Yasmin). She had unprotected intercourse 3 days ago and can’t remember when was the last day she took her pill. She asks you about emergency contraceptive options and other options for contraceptive methods. Her medical history is unremarkable. However, she gained significant weight in the past few years.

stem: Which longer-term contraceptive options would be suitable for Caroline? What factors guided your choices?

options.html: A repeat Yasmin prescription with a phone alarm set around her night shifts
The progestin only mini-pill, being more forgiving of a late or missed dose
The combined transdermal patch, which removes daily dosing altogether
A long acting method, since daily dosing is what failed and weight matters

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Two features of her story drive the choice, and the deck puts both on the case summary slide: ⭐ night shifts with compliance problems, and ⭐ significant weight gain.

>

> Compliance rules out anything daily. That points at the long-acting methods - the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, the etonogestrel implant, or the DMPA injection every three months.

>

> ⚠ B is the trap, and it inverts the truth. The mini-pill is the least forgiving method there is: ⭐ missed by more than 3 hours means backup contraception is needed. For someone working night shifts it is the worst available choice.

>

> C fails on her second feature - ⭐ the patch may be less effective above 90 kg, and it also carries more VTE risk than the pill because it bypasses first-pass metabolism, not less. A repeats what has already failed.

>

> ⚠ One caution worth voicing: the injection and the implant both list weight gain among their effects, and she has raised weight unprompted - so of the long-acting methods the intrauterine system is the one to lead with.

>

> Principle: when adherence is the failure, remove the daily decision - then pick between the long-acting methods on the side effect she cares about.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Patricia is 49-year-old women who presents to your office for counselling on contraceptive methods. She is in a new relationship after a divorce and is sexually active. She reports that her menstrual periods are less regular than previously, she’s been experiencing trouble sleeping for the past 6 months and more acne on her chin. She asks about the risks of using hormonal contraceptives at her age. Patricia is non-smoker. She was diagnosed with hypertension 4 years ago, but it is healthy otherwise. Physical Examination: BMI 24, BP 130/80. Medication Hx: Enalapril (for hypertension), Ibuprofen (as needed for back pain and menstrual cramps)

stem: Does Patricia present a contraindication for combined or progestin-only contraceptive?

options.html: No absolute contraindication - her pressure is controlled, she is a non-smoker
Yes, her hypertension is an absolute contraindication to both types of method here
Yes, her age by itself rules out every hormonal method available to her now
No, and her hypertension has no bearing on the choice between the two types

answer:
The correct answer is A.

⭐ Contraindications are graded on the Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC), and the grade is the answer rather than a yes or no:

>

> ① no restriction · ② advantages generally outweigh the risks · ③ risks usually outweigh the advantages · ④ unacceptable health risk, the true absolute contraindication.

>

> ⭐ Hypertension crosses from relative to absolute at ≥ 160 systolic or ≥ 100 diastolic. Patricia is 130/80 on enalapril, so she is nowhere near that line. She is a non-smoker with a BMI of 24, and she has no migraine with aura and no thromboembolic history - ⭐ the two category ④ entries that matter most, and both apply to combined methods only.

>

> ⚠ D overshoots in the other direction. Her hypertension is not an absolute contraindication, but it is not irrelevant either: it is a genuine consideration on the combined side, and it is one reason a progestin-only method is easy to justify. ⭐ Almost every entry in the combined column is there because of the estrogen, which is why the answer to *"what can she have instead?"* is nearly always progestin-only or intrauterine.

>

> Principle: read hypertension against the 160/100 threshold, and remember the combined column is an estrogen column.

She asks about the risks of using hormonal contraceptives at her age. Patricia is non-smoker. She was diagnosed with hypertension 4 years ago, but it is healthy otherwise. Physical Examination: BMI 24, BP 130/80. Medication Hx: Enalapril (for hypertension), Ibuprofen (as needed for back pain and menstrual cramps)

stem: What are the advantages and disadvantages of combined versus progestin-only contraceptives in Patricia's situation?

options.html: Progestin-only controls her cycle and acne better, but raises her clot risk
Combined treats her cycle, acne and symptoms but adds estrogen risk at 49
Neither has an advantage here, so the decision rests on her preference alone
Combined is contraindicated by her age, so only progestin-only can be offered

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Her three complaints are the advantages column, and her age is the disadvantages column.

>

> What combined offers her. Cycle control for periods that are less regular than they were · ⭐ drospirenone is the anti-androgenic progestin, the one to reach for in hormonal acne - and she has new acne on her chin · and the estrogen helps the perimenopausal symptoms behind her disturbed sleep. The general benefits also apply: ⭐ reduced ovarian and endometrial cancer, reduced dysmenorrhea, lighter and more predictable periods.

>

> What combined costs her. ⭐ Increased VTE risk, and at 49 the background risk is no longer trivial. Her hypertension sits alongside it.

>

> Progestin-only inverts both: ⭐ no increased VTE risk - except the injection, and except drospirenone or cyproterone preparations - but it does little for cycle control and nothing for her acne.

>

> ⚠ A states the trade backwards, which is the point of including it: it is progestin-only that avoids the clot risk, and combined that controls the cycle.

>

> Principle: weigh her symptoms, which want estrogen, against her age and pressure, which do not - and weigh both against the risks of pregnancy, not against zero.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Patricia is 49-year-old women who presents to your office for counselling on contraceptive methods. She is in a new relationship after a divorce and is sexually active. She reports that her menstrual periods are less regular than previously, she’s been experiencing trouble sleeping for the past 6 months and more acne on her chin. She asks about the risks of using hormonal contraceptives at her age. Patricia is non-smoker. She was diagnosed with hypertension 4 years ago, but it is healthy otherwise. Physical Examination: BMI 24, BP 130/80. Medication Hx: Enalapril (for hypertension), Ibuprofen (as needed for back pain and menstrual cramps)

stem: Does the choice of delivery system (pill, injection, intrauterine device) make a difference for Patricia, and why?

options.html: No, because all three deliver equivalent systemic doses of the same hormones
Yes, because only the injection escapes first pass hepatic metabolism entirely
Yes - route changes the estrogen exposure, the adherence needed and the effect
No, provided she is willing to take a tablet at the same time every single day

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Route is not a packaging decision, and three separate things move with it.

>

> - Estrogen exposure. ⭐ The patch and the ring bypass first-pass metabolism, and that - not the dose - is why they carry more VTE risk than the pill. ⚠ B has this exactly backwards: bypassing first pass raises the risk, and the injection is a progestin anyway

> - Adherence. A daily pill, a three-monthly injection and a multi-year device make completely different demands

> - What else it treats. ⭐ The levonorgestrel intrauterine system is listed for heavy bleeding as well as contraception, and is ⭐ more effective than the pill at blocking folliculogenesis because it delivers a high progestin dose at the uterus

>

> ⚠ One caution against the injection at her age: ⭐ DMPA is the exception among progestin-only methods for VTE risk, and the injection and implant may contribute to bone loss - which matters more at 49, approaching menopause, than it would at 25.

>

> Principle: the route decides the estrogen risk, the adherence burden and whether her bleeding gets treated at the same time.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 37-year-old woman has heavy menstrual bleeding and iron-deficiency anemia. She reports nocturia and urinary frequency. Her physician ordered a colonoscopy, ultrasonography and prescribed her a medication to reduce the heavy bleeding while they wait for the results. She takes a combined oral contraceptive and is not planning to become pregnant.

stem: Describe the pharmacological basis underlying the use of tranexamic acid and naproxen to reduce heavy bleeding.

options.html: Both inhibit cyclooxygenase, so both reduce prostaglandin driven uterine cramping
Tranexamic acid inhibits cyclooxygenase; naproxen stabilises the clot that forms
Both act on the endometrium directly, thinning it so that there is less to shed
Tranexamic acid blocks plasminogen binding; naproxen inhibits cyclooxygenase

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Two unrelated mechanisms that happen to converge on the same symptom.

>

> Tranexamic acid is an ⭐ antifibrinolytic: it blocks the plasminogen lysine-binding site, so plasminogen is not converted to plasmin, so ⭐ the clot that has formed is not broken down. It does nothing to the cause - ⭐ it is symptomatic only, which is exactly why it suits a patient who is waiting for results.

>

> Naproxen is a non-selective NSAID: it ⭐ reduces prostaglandin synthesis through non-selective cyclooxygenase inhibition, which reduces uterine cramping and also reduces heavy bleeding. That it treats her cramps at the same time is a convenience rather than a coincidence.

>

> ⭐ Neither shrinks a fibroid, and neither treats a cause - and that is the setup for the next question in the case, where the ultrasound comes back.

>

> Principle: tranexamic acid protects the clot, naproxen removes the prostaglandins - both buy time, neither changes the diagnosis.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 37-year-old woman has heavy menstrual bleeding and iron-deficiency anemia. She reports nocturia and urinary frequency. Her physician ordered a colonoscopy, ultrasonography and prescribed her a medication to reduce the heavy bleeding while they wait for the results. She takes a combined oral contraceptive and is not planning to become pregnant.

stem: Does this patient present any contraindications to these drugs?

options.html: Yes - her combined pill plus an antifibrinolytic compounds clot risk
Yes, her iron deficiency anemia is an absolute contraindication to both agents
No, neither drug carries any contraindication relevant to this patient at all
Yes, her urinary frequency indicates the renal impairment that rules out both

answer:
The correct answer is A.

⭐ The contraindication to tranexamic acid is a history of venous thromboembolism, and she has no such history - but she takes a combined oral contraceptive, and ⭐ combined hormonal contraception raises VTE risk by increasing factors VII, VIII, IX and X. Layering an antifibrinolytic on top of a prothrombotic pill is the interaction worth naming, and it is one the case sets up deliberately by telling you she is on a COC.

>

> For naproxen, the contraindications are ⭐ severe kidney disease, gastritis or peptic ulcer, and coagulopathies. None is stated for her.

>

> ⚠ D is the specific trap. Her nocturia and urinary frequency are pressure symptoms from the fibroids pressing on the bladder - the ultrasound confirms it two slides later. Reading them as renal impairment mistakes a mass effect for a creatinine. B inverts the logic: her anemia is the reason to treat, not a reason not to.

>

> Principle: read her medication list as part of the contraindication check, and read urinary symptoms in a fibroid case as pressure until proven otherwise.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A week later the results were available. The colonoscopy is negative. Ultrasonography shows a modestly enlarged uterus with three uterine fibroids.

stem: Which of the following drugs can be used to reduce the size of fibroids (select all that apply), and what is the pharmacological basis for their effect?

options.html: The intrauterine device, leuprolide and relugolix

answer:
The correct answer is B.

⚠ The source asks this as a select-all, which the house rule does not bank - so it is written here as a combinations question with the same content.

>

> ⭐ Only the GnRH-directed drugs shrink a fibroid. Everything else on the list treats the bleeding.

>

> | Drug | Effect on fibroid size | Why |

> | --- | --- | --- |

> | Tranexamic acid | none | antifibrinolytic, ⭐ symptomatic only |

> | Ibuprofen | none | reduces prostaglandins, so cramping and flow |

> | Levonorgestrel IUD | none | listed for heavy bleeding, not for size |

> | Leuprolide (agonist) | ⭐ yes | continuous dosing causes an initial flare, then receptor desensitisation and suppression |

> | Relugolix (antagonist) | ⭐ yes | ⭐ immediate receptor blockade - faster onset and NO flare, since no downregulation is needed |

>

> Both work the same way in the end: shut down gonadotropins, so the ovary stops making estrogen, so the estrogen-dependent fibroid shrinks. ⚠ The flare matters clinically - a GnRH agonist can transiently worsen a hormone-driven lesion before it helps, and an antagonist never does.

>

> Principle: fibroids are estrogen-dependent, so only the drugs that remove estrogen change their size.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: After her diagnosis, she was prescribed Relugolix/estradiol/norethindrone acetate (a combination of a GnRH antagonist and low doses of steroid sex hormones).

stem: Why was estradiol and norethindrone added to her therapy?

options.html: To provide contraception, which the GnRH antagonist does not itself supply
To enhance the antagonist's effect on the fibroid by adding a second pathway
To offset the hypoestrogenic state, above all the bone loss it would cause
To prevent the initial gonadotropin flare that a GnRH antagonist would cause

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Relugolix works by producing a hypoestrogenic state, and that state is the treatment and the problem at once.

>

> ⭐ The hypoestrogenic profile is: bone loss, hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, and mood and sleep change. Of those, ⭐ bone loss is the one that limits how long the drug can be given, because it is cumulative and silent.

>

> Giving back a low dose of estradiol with a progestin restores enough estrogen to protect the skeleton and settle the vasomotor symptoms, while leaving too little to re-grow the fibroid. The norethindrone is there for the usual reason a progestin accompanies estrogen: ⭐ unopposed estrogen drives endometrial hyperplasia, so a woman with a uterus needs the progestin alongside it.

>

> ⚠ D describes the wrong drug class. ⭐ Antagonists never flare - that is an agonist problem, and it is one of the reasons to choose relugolix over leuprolide.

>

> ⚠ The vault note does not use the term "add-back" or carry this combination product by name, so the reasoning above is built from its hypoestrogenic adverse-effect profile rather than quoted. Worth confirming with the facilitator.

>

> Principle: you are deliberately inducing a menopause, so you give back just enough estrogen to protect the bone without feeding the fibroid.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: After her diagnosis, she was prescribed Relugolix/estradiol/norethindrone acetate (a combination of a GnRH antagonist and low doses of steroid sex hormones).

stem: Would she need to stop taking her combined oral contraceptives? Why?

options.html: No, the two are complementary and should deliberately be taken alongside it
No, but only if she reduces her combined pill to alternate days instead
Yes, since the combined pill would provoke a flare from the antagonist
Yes - the regimen already holds estrogen and a progestin, duplicating both

answer:
The correct answer is D.

The prescription is already three drugs in one tablet: a GnRH antagonist plus low doses of estradiol and norethindrone. Continuing a combined oral contraceptive on top means a second estrogen and a second progestin.

>

> Two problems follow:

>

> - The dose is the point. The added steroids are deliberately low - enough to protect bone, ⭐ too little to feed an estrogen-dependent fibroid. Adding a contraceptive dose of ethinyl estradiol on top defeats the reason the combination exists

> - Stacked estrogen is stacked risk, and ⭐ the VTE risk of combined hormonal contraception is its principal harm

>

> ⚠ D invents a mechanism. ⭐ Antagonists do not flare, and a combined pill would not cause one.

>

> ⚠ What this answer cannot settle is contraception. She is not planning to become pregnant, and the vault note does not state whether this combination is itself contraceptive - so stopping the pill leaves a question about what replaces it for that purpose, and a non-hormonal method is the obvious candidate. ⭐ Flagging that gap is part of the answer; filling it from outside the lecture is not.

>

> Principle: the add-back dose is calibrated, so anything stacked on top breaks the calibration - and stopping a contraceptive raises a contraceptive question.

> ⚠ Worth noticing what the stem withholds: it never gives her age, and never states her Tanner stage explicitly. "Thin, athletic" is doing different work - it is the ⭐ functional hypothalamic hint the article returns to later.

> Principle: 13 without development, 15 with - and the workbook's 16 is a different source, not a correction.

stem: A 14-year-old girl comes in with a history of monthly cyclical abdominal pain. On examination, you note midline tenderness in the area below the umbilicus, and a purplish bulging at the vaginal introitus. Of the following, the most likely diagnosis is:
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Every element is the outflow-tract column of the amenorrhea table.

>

> - ⭐ Cyclical pain with no bleeding is that column's named clue - the endometrium is cycling normally, blood is made but cannot get out

> - Purplish bulging at the introitus is retained blood behind an ⭐ imperforate hymen, the commonest outflow tract abnormality (1 in 2000)

> - Midline suprapubic tenderness is the distended vagina and uterus above it

>

> ⚠ The vault teaches this under hematometra and imperforate hymen rather than the word "hematocolpos" - colpos is the vagina, metra the uterus, and the same obstruction produces both.

>

> A has no uterus, so no cyclical pain and no trapped blood. B, C and E are not cyclical and not midline-obstructive; torsion in particular is acute and unilateral, not monthly.

>

> Principle: monthly pain with no period means the blood is being made and cannot leave - look at the introitus.

stem: A 15-year-old girl comes in for evaluation of infrequent menstrual periods. On examination, you note a BMI of 35 and acne. Otherwise, her examination is unremarkable. Of the following, what is the most likely laboratory abnormality associated with this patient's presentation?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Obesity + acne + infrequent rather than absent periods is the ⭐ eugonadotropic anovulation column, and that is where PCOS lives.

>

> The table's clues for it are exactly these: ⭐ hirsutism, acne, obesity, and cycles irregular rather than absent - and its next test is ⭐ testosterone, DHEA-S and 17-OHP. An elevated free testosterone is what that testing is looking for.

>

> A would mean the ovary has failed, which gives absent periods and vasomotor symptoms. D and E share a branch - ⭐ low T4 raises TRH, which raises both TSH and prolactin, and prolactin then suppresses GnRH - but neither explains obesity with acne. C is not a measurable clinical test.

>

> Principle: irregular rather than absent, with androgenic signs, is anovulation - and the androgen is what you measure.

stem: A 16-year-old girl is seen with a complaint of excessive bleeding with menses (menorrhagia). Of the following, which component of the history and examination most suggests von Willebrand disease?

options.html: Heavy flow from time of initial menses.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

⭐ The discriminator is that it has been heavy since the very first period. An inherited bleeding disorder has been present her whole life, so there was never a normal baseline - whereas an acquired or structural cause has a before and an after.

>

> vWD sits in the ⭐ C - coagulopathy letter of PALM-COEIN, and it is the one to think of in an adolescent, because menarche is often the first haemostatic challenge she has ever faced.

>

> A points at immaturity of the axis, which is ⭐ the commonest cause of irregular bleeding in the first couple of years after menarche and is the competing answer here - but anovulatory bleeding is irregular, not uniformly heavy from the start. C suggests a structural or hormonal cause. D and E point elsewhere entirely.

>

> Principle: heavy from the first period ever is inherited until proven otherwise; heavy after a normal history is acquired.

stem: Of the following, which is the most appropriate first-line therapy for primary dysmenorrhea?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

⭐ Primary dysmenorrhea is prostaglandin-mediated, so the first-line treatment is the one that stops prostaglandin synthesis.

>

> The pharmacology lecture puts it directly: NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin synthesis through non-selective cyclooxygenase inhibition, reducing uterine cramping, with dysmenorrhea named as the indication.

>

> ⚠ D is the strongest distractor and is not wrong in general - combined oral contraceptives are listed for dysmenorrhea too, and the lecture names it among their benefits. It is second line here: an NSAID is cheaper, immediate, taken only around the period, and needed for a trial before escalating. A has no anti-prostaglandin effect. C treats infection, which would make this secondary dysmenorrhea.

>

> Principle: primary dysmenorrhea is prostaglandins, so block them first and reach for the pill when that fails.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Jessica is a 14 year old female coming to see you because she is concerned she has not started her period.

stem: Jessica is a 14 year old female coming to see you because she is concerned she has not started her period. What is the most first important thing to help guide intervention?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

⭐ Breast development is the clinical readout of estrogen exposure, and estrogen status is what splits the differential before any blood test.

>

> - Thelarche present - the axis has worked, so at 14 she is inside the window (the threshold is 15 with secondary sex characteristics) and the question becomes outflow tract

> - Thelarche absent - the threshold is 13 without them, so she is already past it, and the problem is the ovary or above

>

> ⚠ A is the trap, and the distinction is worth holding. ⭐ Pubic hair is adrenal (adrenarche); breast development is ovarian (thelarche). Pubic hair can appear normally while the ovary does nothing - which is exactly the pattern in Erika's case later in this quiz, Tanner I breast with Tanner II pubic hair.

>

> C comes after the examination, not before it. D matters for short stature.

>

> Principle: stage the breast before you measure anything - it tells you whether estrogen has ever been present.

stem: Kaitlyn is a 16 year old female with a past medical history of type I diabetes. She comes to you today with concerns of irregular periods. She has not had her period for the past 3 months. Physical exam is unremarkable. The most important thing to rule out is:
answer:
The correct answer is D.

⭐ Rule out pregnancy first, before any other test and whatever the story sounds like. The vault states it twice over - "1st thing to rule out is PREGNANCY !!" and "beta hCG before anything else" - and it is the top branch of the whole flowchart.

>

> ⭐ Three months without menses after regular cycles is the definition of secondary amenorrhea, so this is not merely irregularity.

>

> ⚠ Her diabetes is there to pull you off it. Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune and travels with thyroid disease and primary ovarian insufficiency, so it invites a workup - but none of that changes what comes first. A, B and C are all reasonable entries on the differential and all of them are tested after the hCG.

>

> Principle: the test order is not the likelihood order - pregnancy is excluded first because missing it is the costliest error.

stem: Maggie is a 16 year old female who you are seeing for primary amenorrhea. Her physical exam and investigations are normal to date. A progesterone withdrawal test was performed and resulted in menstruation. The correct interpretation of this result is:

options.html: There is an intact hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and patent outflow tract

answer:
The correct answer is C.

A withdrawal bleed is a functional test of three things at once, and passing it clears all three:

>

> - ⭐ There is estrogen - the progestin had a primed, proliferated endometrium to withdraw from. No estrogen means no lining, so nothing to shed

> - ⭐ The outflow tract is patent - the blood reached the outside

> - The axis is working well enough to have produced that estrogen

>

> What it shows is missing is ovulation, and therefore progesterone - which is the eugonadotropic anovulation column: ⭐ no ovulation → no progesterone → no withdrawal bleed, until you supply the progestin yourself.

>

> ⚠ B is the subtle one. She *is* short of progesterone, which is why the test works - but the option as written describes a systemic deficiency state, and the interpretation the test licenses is the positive one in C. A is what a negative test would suggest.

>

> Principle: a positive withdrawal bleed proves estrogen and a patent tract; what it reveals is anovulation.

stem: Lisa is 16 years old presenting with irregular periods. You have diagnosed her with PCOS. She is sexually active, and uses condoms regularly. You emphasize the importance of contraception despite the irregular menses. What is the best choice for contraception in this patient?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The combined pill is the answer because it does ⭐ three jobs at once in PCOS, and the vault names it as the treatment: COC or cyclic progestin - oppose the estrogen, protect the endometrium.

>

> - Contraception, which is what she came for

> - Cycle regulation for the irregular menses

> - ⭐ Endometrial protection. Anovulation leaves estrogen unopposed, and unopposed estrogen is the pathway to hyperplasia - the reason PCOS needs treating even when she does not want to conceive

> - And a fourth: the anti-androgenic benefit for acne and hirsutism, strongest with drospirenone

>

> ⚠ A is genuinely defensible and worth arguing in the room. The levonorgestrel IUS is more effective contraception and protects the endometrium well - it is listed for heavy bleeding too. It does not regulate the cycle or help the androgenic features, and it is more invasive for a 16-year-old. ⭐ The CHSG guide says outright that some questions may have more than one acceptable response, and this is one.

>

> C causes weight gain and may contribute to bone loss, both poor choices in an adolescent with PCOS. D is unreliable.

>

> Principle: in PCOS the pill is contraception, cycle control, endometrial protection and acne treatment in one decision.

stem: Patricia is a 13 year old female who presents with a complaint of heavy periods. She started her period 3 months ago and finds that it last 7-9 days, and she has to change her pad every 2-3 hours. On exam, you notice petechiae on her lower legs. The most appropriate first test is:
answer:
The correct answer is A.

⭐ The petechiae are the whole question. Heavy periods from menarche would already raise a coagulopathy; petechiae make it the leading diagnosis, and they point specifically at a platelet problem rather than a factor problem.

>

> A CBC answers two things in one cheap test:

>

> - The platelet count - thrombocytopenia, including ITP and leukemia, which the vault lists in the C - coagulopathy letter of PALM-COEIN

> - The haemoglobin - how much this bleeding has actually cost her, which decides urgency

>

> ⚠ Her bleeding is objectively heavy, not just described that way: ⭐ soaking a pad every 2-3 hours, for 7-9 days. The vault's AUB examination list names bruising and petechiae as the finding that signals coagulopathy.

>

> B and C investigate an axis that is producing periods perfectly well. D looks for structure in a 13-year-old three months post-menarche, where structural lesions are rare.

>

> Principle: petechiae plus heavy menses from menarche is a platelet count before anything else.

stem: Jackie is a 16 year old female who is presenting with complaints of irregular periods. What is the most important thing to establish?

options.html: Levels of FSH, LH, TSH and prolactin

answer:
The correct answer is C.

⭐ Time since menarche is what decides whether this is a disease at all. Cycles in the first couple of years after the first period are commonly anovulatory, because the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis is still maturing - irregularity then is physiological.

>

> So the same complaint means two different things:

>

> | Menarche | Irregular cycles mean |

> | --- | --- |

> | Recent, within about 2 years | ⭐ normal immaturity of the axis - reassure and follow |

> | Years ago, cycles once regular | a change that needs a cause |

>

> ⚠ A is the right answer to a different question. Secondary sexual traits matter when periods have never started, as in Jessica's case at the top of this quiz. Jackie is menstruating, so development has plainly occurred. D is where the workup goes after this question is answered, and ordering it first risks investigating normal puberty. B matters for short stature.

>

> Principle: ask when the first period was - it separates an immature axis from a real disorder.

stem: Sonya is a 17 year old female who is presenting with complaints of infrequent periods. Menarche was 13 years of age. She has never been sexually active. She points out some discolouration on the back of her neck that she noticed a few months ago. On exam, she is well grown with a BMI of 29. She is Tanner stage 5 for breast and pubic hair development. Heart, lung and abdominal exam are benign aside from striae on her abdomen. She has acne on her back and face. Neurologic exam is normal. Blood work is pending. Most likely diagnosis based on the provided information?

options.html: Unable to say - need blood work

answer:
The correct answer is A.

⭐ The discolouration on the back of her neck is acanthosis nigricans, and it is the sign the stem is built around - velvety hyperpigmentation in the flexures, a marker of insulin resistance.

>

> Put beside it: infrequent periods (anovulation), BMI 29, acne on back and face (hyperandrogenism), fully developed at Tanner 5 so the axis works. That is the vault's PCOS clue list - ⭐ hirsutism, acne, obesity, and cycles irregular rather than absent - and PCOS is ⭐ the commonest secondary cause of amenorrhea at 28%.

>

> ⚠ B is the answer the question is testing you against. PCOS is a clinical diagnosis, and the Rotterdam pattern - irregular cycles plus clinical hyperandrogenism - is already satisfied by what is in front of you. Bloods confirm and exclude; they do not create the diagnosis.

>

> C would bring galactorrhea and a normal BMI, and the vault notes hyperprolactinemia is as often a drug as a tumour. D describes her metabolic risk, and the striae and acanthosis fit it, but ⚠ metabolic syndrome does not cause infrequent periods - it is the company PCOS keeps, not the diagnosis.

>

> Principle: anovulation plus clinical hyperandrogenism is PCOS before the bloods come back, and acanthosis names the mechanism.

stem: What is the underlying mechanism of amenorrhea in hyperprolactinemia?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

⭐ Prolactin acts at the top of the axis: it suppresses GnRH pulses, and everything downstream follows from that.

>

> The vault's chain is explicit: ↓ T4 → ↑ TRH → ↑ TSH and ↑ prolactin → prolactin suppresses GnRH pulses → anovulation.

>

> ⚠ B and C are the near-misses, and the distinction is the point of the question. LH and FSH do fall - but as a consequence of losing the GnRH drive above them, not because prolactin acts on the gonadotroph. ⭐ The pituitary is obeying a hypothalamus that has gone quiet, which is also why this is classified as hypogonadotropic and why it is reversible when the prolactin is treated. A is downstream again - estrogen falls because the ovary is not being stimulated.

>

> Worth carrying: hyperprolactinemia is present in ⭐ 10% of amenorrhoeic women and 50% of those with galactorrhoea, and the first-line treatment for a prolactinoma is a ⭐ dopamine agonist, not surgery.

>

> Principle: prolactin silences GnRH - the low gonadotropins and low estrogen are both consequences, not the lesion.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Erika is 14 year old girl who you are seeing for amenorrhea. She has not yet started her period. She reports that she is previously healthy but is getting bullied in school because she hasn't started to “develop”. On exam, she is Tanner stage I for breast development and Tanner stage II for pubic hair. You note subtle dysmorphic features. Remainder of her exam is unremarkable. Her growth chart is shown.

stem: What is the most appropriate next test?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

⭐ FSH is the single number that splits the differential, and this stem and the next are deliberately a pair: this one asks what to do next, the next asks what makes the diagnosis.

>

> The vault puts it plainly: ⭐ high FSH means the ovary has failed; low FSH means the problem is above it.

>

> Erika's picture points hard at the ovarian column - Tanner I breast (no estrogen) with Tanner II pubic hair (adrenarche has happened, so the adrenal is fine), subtle dysmorphic features, and a growth chart. That is ⭐ Turner syndrome, the commonest cause of primary amenorrhea at 27%, whose clues are listed as short stature, webbed neck, shield chest.

>

> A and C belong to a short-stature workup, and would be reasonable if growth were the only issue - but she has absent puberty with dysmorphism, which is a different question. D measures the downstream consequence rather than the level that localises the lesion.

>

> Principle: in absent puberty, FSH first - it tells you whether to look at the ovary or above it.

>

> Principle: FSH localises, karyotype diagnoses - and in Turner the karyotype also decides what happens to the gonads.

She has been sexually active with her boyfriend but uses condoms. She occasionally drinks alcohol on the weekends and has experimented with Ecstasy. She is a B student. She exercises 6-7 days per week. On exam, she is Tanner stage V for breast and pubic hair. Exam is otherwise unremarkable. Growth chart is shown.

stem: The most important initial first test is:
answer:
The correct answer is B.

⭐ Rule out pregnancy first, before any other test and whatever the story sounds like. It is the top branch of the vault's flowchart and its first high-yield discriminator.

>

> ⚠ "Primary amenorrhea" makes this feel wrong, and that is the trap. Never having menstruated does not exclude pregnancy: ovulation precedes the first period, so conception is possible before menarche. She is sexually active, and condoms are a method with real typical-use failure.

>

> C is the number that splits the differential, but it comes after the hCG. D sits on the branch below FSH. A would answer whether she has a uterus, which her Tanner V development already makes likely.

>

> Principle: primary amenorrhea does not exempt a sexually active 16-year-old from a pregnancy test.

stem: Which of the following will be most helpful in this context?

options.html: Serum FSH, LSH, prolactin, thyroid function
Serum FSH, LH, thyroid function, karyotype
Perform a pelvic ultrasound and pelvic exam

answer:
The correct answer is B.

With pregnancy excluded, the next layer is the one the flowchart runs in parallel: ⭐ prolactin and TSH first, then FSH.

>

> - Prolactin and thyroid share a branch for a mechanistic reason - ⭐ low T4 raises TRH, which raises both TSH and prolactin, and prolactin then suppresses GnRH. Two common, treatable, reversible causes

> - FSH then localises: ⭐ high means the ovary has failed, low means the problem is above it

>

> ⚠ The option contains a typo - "LSH" for LH - and it is the source's, reproduced as written.

>

> A is the androgen panel, which belongs on the anovulation branch and is not yet indicated in a girl with no hyperandrogenic signs. C adds a karyotype before there is a high FSH to justify it - ⭐ the vault orders karyotype only when FSH is high. D is the step after this one.

>

> Principle: prolactin and thyroid are the cheap reversible causes; FSH is the number that localises.

The bloods are normal, so the question becomes anatomy: the flowchart's second branch is ⭐ "uterus present?", and that is answered by imaging and examination rather than by more serum.

>

> It matters even with Tanner V development, because the two conditions it separates both present exactly like this:

>

> | | MRKH | Androgen insensitivity |

> | --- | --- | --- |

> | Karyotype | 46,XX | 46,XY |

> | Pubic hair | present | ⭐ absent |

> | Testosterone | female range | male range |

>

>

>

> Principle: when the hormones are normal and she has developed, look for the uterus.

She exercises 6-7 days per week. On exam, she is Tanner stage V for breast and pubic hair. Exam is otherwise unremarkable. Growth chart is shown. Before you can order tests in a logical sequence, you find out your resident has ordered multiple tests. The serum testosterone, DHEAS, LH/FSH ratio, prolactin and thyroid function is normal. Serum FSH and LH are low. Genital exam is within normal limits. Karyotype and ultrasound are normal.

stem: Your next step is:

options.html: Perform a MRI of the head
Perform a MRI of the abdomen

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Low FSH and LH puts her in the ⭐ hypothalamic / hypogonadotropic column, and the vault's instruction for that column is unambiguous: ⭐ functional causes first, MRI only if no stressor - and its investigation list warns ⚠ MRI is not first line.

>

> She has an obvious stressor: she ⭐ exercises 6-7 days per week, which is the column's own named clue - low BMI, athlete, recent stressor. So the imaging that A proposes is precisely what the note says to hold back.

>

> The progesterone challenge is the right next move, and one of the CHSG's stated objectives is to know its indications. It answers whether there is enough estrogen to have primed an endometrium: a bleed means estrogen is present and the tract is patent; ⭐ no bleed points to a deeper hypoestrogenic state, which is what sustained energy deficit produces.

>

> ⚠ The OCR of this option dropped its letter - the source reads ) Perform a progesterone challenge. Transcribed as C from its position.

>

> D screens for late-onset CAH, which belongs on the anovulation branch and is already unlikely with normal androgens.

>

> Principle: low gonadotropins with a stressor in the history is functional until excluded - scan last, not first.

preamble.html: Jennifer is 16 year old female who presents with primary amenorrhea. She is previously healthy and has had no surgeries. She has been sexually active with her boyfriend but uses condoms. She occasionally drinks alcohol on the weekends and has experimented with Ecstasy. She is a B student. She exercises 6-7 days per week. On exam, she is Tanner stage V for breast and pubic hair. Exam is otherwise unremarkable. Growth chart is shown. Before you can order tests in a logical sequence, you find out your resident has ordered multiple tests. The serum testosterone, DHEAS, LH/FSH ratio, prolactin and thyroid function is normal. Serum FSH and LH are low. Genital exam is within normal limits. Karyotype and ultrasound are normal.

stem: The most likely diagnosis is:
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Everything has been excluded except the thing that was in the social history from the start.

>

> | Finding | What it rules out |

> | --- | --- |

> | Low FSH and LH | ⭐ Turner - ovarian failure gives HIGH FSH |

> | Normal karyotype, normal genital exam | AIS, which is 46,XY with absent pubic hair |

> | Normal testosterone, DHEAS, 46,XX | CAH, which is hyperandrogenic |

> | Tanner V, normal ultrasound | an outflow or developmental cause |

>

> What remains is ⭐ functional hypothalamic amenorrhea - 15% of secondary amenorrhea, whose triggers the vault lists as eating disorder, exercise, stress. Exercising 6-7 days per week is the mechanism: sustained energy deficit shuts down GnRH pulses, so gonadotropins fall and the ovary is never asked to work.

>

> ⚠ The treatment is not hormonal first. The vault says ⭐ restore energy availability, with HRT only if it persists - and notes that ⭐ estrogen deficiency costs bone whatever the compartment, which is why this is not a benign diagnosis in a 16-year-old still building peak bone mass.

>

> Principle: low gonadotropins with a normal everything else and an athlete's history is functional - and the treatment is energy, not estrogen.
